akhfash:1-1.t:
As for His words ﴿الۤمۤ﴾, these letters were made vowelless because the speech is not run together (mudraj); it would only be run together if it were conjoined by a conjunction. That is because the Arabs say all the letters of the alphabet with pause when they do not insert conjunctions, saying "ألفْ باءْ تاءْ ثاءْ", and they say "ألفٌ وباءٌ وتاءٌ وثاءٌ". Likewise numbers for them, as long as they do not insert conjunctions: [so] they say "واحدْ اثنانْ ثلاثَهْ" (one, two, three). And [this shows] that it is not run together: the alif of "اثنين" is made disjunctive although it is a connecting alif. If it were connected to what precedes it, it would go; but this is counting, and in counting and in letters each one is something separated on its own. Similar to that are ﴿الۤمۤصۤ﴾, ﴿الۤر﴾, ﴿الۤمۤر﴾, ﴿كۤهيعۤصۤ﴾, ﴿طسۤمۤ﴾, ﴿يسۤ﴾, ﴿طه﴾, ﴿حـمۤ﴾, ﴿قۤ﴾ and ﴿صۤ﴾. However, some people put ﴿يسۤ﴾, ﴿طه﴾ and ﴿حـمۤ﴾ in the accusative, and this is frequent in the speech of the Arabs. That is because they made them nouns like the foreign nouns "هابيل" (Abel) and "قابيل" (Cain). Either they put them in an accusative position without declining them [i.e. as diptotes], as though he said "اذكر حم وطس ويس" (mention Ḥā-Mīm, Ṭā-Sīn and Yā-Sīn); or they made them like the nouns that are not fully declinable, giving their ending one fixed vowel, like the fatḥa of "أينَ", and like some people's saying ﴿ٱلْحَمْدِ للَّهِ﴾. Some read ﴿صَ﴾, ﴿نَ﴾ and ﴿قَ﴾ with fatḥa, making them nouns that are not fully declinable, binding them to one vowel, and making them names of the sūra*, so they became feminine nouns. Some Arabs do not decline a feminine noun whose middle letter is vowelless, such as "هِنْد", "جُمْل" and "دَعد"**. The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; this is the fourth evidentiary verse]:
وإني لأَهوى بيت هِنْدٍ وأهلها * على هنواتٍ قد ذكرن على هِنْدِ
(I love Hind's house and her people, despite the faults that have been told against Hind.)
[Translator's note: the asterisks * and ** appear thus in the source.]
It is permissible in this dialect; or he may have named it with the letter, and the letter is masculine, and when a feminine is named with a masculine name it is not declined; [so] he made ﴿صۤ﴾ and the like a name of the sūra, did not decline it, and put it in an accusative position.
Some said "صادِ والقرآنِ", taking it from "صاديت" (I confronted), then [forming] an imperative, as you say "رامِ" (contend), as if he said "صادِ الحقَّ بعملك" (confront the truth with your deeds), i.e. aim for it; then He said ﴿وَٱلْقُرْآنِ﴾, swearing an oath; then He said ﴿بَلِ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ فِي عِزَّةٍ وَشِقَاقٍ﴾. It is on this that the oath falls. That is because they claimed that "بل" here is really "إنّ", and therefore the oath became [an oath] on it.
People have differed about the letters at the openings of the sūras. Some said: "They are only letters with which [the sūra] is opened." If it is said: "Can there be anything in the Quran that has no meaning?", [the answer is that] the meaning of these is that He began with them so that it would be known that the preceding sūra had ended and that He had started on another. So this was made a sign of the break between them. That is found in the speech of the Arabs: a man among them recites poetry and says [in the rajaz metre; this is the fifth evidentiary verse]:
* بلْ. وبلدةٍ ما الانسُ من أُهّالها *
(Nay — and many a land whose inhabitants are not humans.)
or he says [in the rajaz metre; this is the sixth evidentiary verse]:
* بلْ. ما هاجَ أحزاناً وشجواً قد شجا *
(Nay — what stirred up sorrows and a grief that has grieved.)
"بل" is not part of the verse and is not counted in its metre; rather, one speech is cut off by it and another begun. Others said: "They are letters which, when joined, spell something whose meaning is known, and some people were given knowledge of that." That is because some of them used to say: "ألر", "حم" and "ن": this is the name "الرحمن" (the All-Merciful), Majestic and Mighty is He; and the rest of them are of this kind.
They said that His words ﴿كۤهيعۤصۤ﴾ are "كاف هاد عالم صادق" (Sufficient, Guide, Knowing, Truthful): He made one letter of each of these names explicit so that it would point to them. This shows that the first view cannot hold unless it has a meaning, because he means the meaning of the letters. [Translator's note: so in the source; the sense is obscure.] They did not make any of these letters accusative other than those I mentioned to you, because ﴿الۤمۤ﴾, ﴿طسۤمۤ﴾ and ﴿كۤهيعۤصۤ﴾ are not like any of the nouns; they are only disconnected letters.
He said ﴿الۤمۤ﴾ ﴿ٱللَّهُ لاَ إِلَـٰهَ إِلاَّ هُوَ ﴾: the mīm has fatḥa because a vowelless letter met it, so it had to be given a vowel. If it is said: "Why was it not given the genitive vowel (kasra)?" — that is not required in it; [and] they only wanted a vowel, and when they gave it any vowel at all they reached the speech by it. Had it been given kasra it would have been permissible, though I know it only as a dialect form.
Some said: "They gave fatḥa to the letters of spelling when a vowelless letter met them, to distinguish them from other [words]." And they said "مِنَ الرجل" (from the man), giving fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, and they say "هلِ الرجل" and "بلِ الرجل", and there is no difference between these two and "من الرجل", except that they gave fatḥa in "مِنَ الرجل" so that two kasras would not come together. Yet they gave kasra in ﴿إِذِ ٱلظَّالِمُونَ﴾, where two kasras have come together, because "مِن" is used more often in their speech than "إذْ", so they gave it fatḥa to make it light for them. If you wish, you may say that "ألم" are letters separated from one another, because there is no conjunction among them, and they are also separated from what follows them; so the basic form is to say ﴿الم ألله﴾, making the alif of ﴿الله﴾ disjunctive, since what precedes it is separated from it, just as you said "واحد، إثنان" with a disjunctive alif; and just as the Quran readers read ﴿نۤ وَٱلْقَلَمِ﴾ pronouncing the nūn clearly, because it is separated. If it were not separated it would not be pronounced clearly, unless one of the six letters met it. Do you not see that you say "خذه من زيد" (take it from Zayd) and "خذه من عمرو" (take it from ʿAmr), pronouncing the nūn clearly in "عمرو" and not in "زيد"? So since it is a vowelless mīm followed by a disjunctive letter with fatḥa, it is permissible to give the mīm the fatḥa of the alif and drop the alif, in the dialect of those who say "منَ ابوك" (who is your father?), so that it is not disjunctive. Some people treated (نون) as run together and said ﴿نونَ والقلمِ﴾, keeping the nūn but not pronouncing it clearly; and they said ﴿يسۤ وَٱلْقُرْآنِ﴾, again without pronouncing it clearly. This nūn here is not * like His words ﴿كۤهيعۤصۤ﴾, ﴿طسۤ تِلْكَ﴾ and ﴿حـمۤ عۤسۤقۤ﴾: [for] these nūns are not pronounced clearly in anyone's reading, because the nūn is close to the ṣād, since the ṣād and the nūn are from the articulation point of the tip of the tongue. Likewise the tāʾ and the sīn in ﴿طسۤ تِلْكَ﴾ and in ﴿حـمۤ عۤسۤقۤ﴾; therefore the nūn was not pronounced clearly, since they are close to it. The nūn was pronounced clearly in ﴿يسۤ﴾ and ﴿نون﴾ because of the distance between the nūn and the wāw, since the nūn is with the tip of the tongue and the wāw is with the lips.

akhfash:2-2.t:
He said ﴿لاَ رَيْبَ فِيهِ هُدًى لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ and He said ﴿فَلاۤ إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ﴾, making both accusative (manṣūb) without nunation. That is because every indefinite noun that you negate with "لا", placing "لا" next to the noun, takes fatḥa without nunation, because "لا" is likened to a verb, just as "إنْ" and "ما" were likened to a verb. (فيه) is in the position of its khabar (predicate), and its khabar is nominative; it is like the fāʿil (agent), the accusative [noun] has become like the mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and (لا) is like the verb. The nunation was dropped from it only because you made it and "لا" a single noun, and any two things made into one noun are not declined. The fatḥa in it belongs to the whole noun; it is built on it (mabnī) and made not fully declinable. The noun after "لا" is in an accusative position, governed by "لا".
As for His words ﴿لاَ خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلاَ هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ﴾, the proper way in it is the nominative, because what the second is conjoined to can only be nominative, and you made it nominative in order to conjoin the second to it. Some people read it in the accusative, and made the second [nominative] as a mubtadaʾ (subject).
His words ﴿فَلاَ رَفَثَ وَلاَ فُسُوقَ وَلاَ جِدَالَ فِي ٱلْحَجِّ﴾: the proper way is the accusative, because this is negation and because it is all indefinite. Some people said ﴿فَلاَ رَفَثٌ وَلاَ فُسُوقٌ وَلاَ جِدَالٌ فِي ٱلْحَجِّ﴾, making all of it nominative; that is because in some of the speech of the Arabs all of this accusative may be nominative. The poet said [in the basīṭ metre; this is the seventh evidentiary verse]:
وما صرمتُكِ حتى قلتِ معلنةً * لا ناقةٌ ليَ في هذا ولا جَمَل
(I did not cut you off until you said openly: "I have neither she-camel nor he-camel in this [affair].")
This is an answer to someone saying "هل فيه رفثٌ أو فسوقٌ" (is there obscenity or wickedness in it?): he made the nouns nominative as mubtadaʾ and gave them a khabar, therefore its answer is nominative. When he says "لا شيءَ" (nothing), it is only an answer to "هل من شىءٍ" (is there anything?), because in "هل مِن شيءٍ"* the "مِن" has governed [the noun] in the genitive and the khabar is implied, while the position is nominative — like "بحسبِك أَنْ تشتمَني" (it is enough for you to insult me), [which] is really "حسبُك أَنْ تشتمني": the position is nominative, while the bāʾ has governed. [Translator's note: the asterisk appears thus in the source.]
Some people said ﴿فَلاَ رَفَثٌ وَلاَ فُسُوقٌ وَلاَ جِدَالَ فِي ٱلْحَجِّ﴾, making the first nominative, according to what is permitted of the nominative in this, or as a prohibition, as though He said "فلا يكونن فيه رفثٌ ولا فسوقٌ" (let there be no obscenity or wickedness in it) — as you say "سمعُكَ اليّ" (your hearing to me, i.e. listen to me), which the Arabs say in the nominative, and as you say to a man**: "حسبُك" (enough for you) and "كفاك" (that suffices you). And he made "الجدال" [accusative] as negation. [Translator's note: the double asterisk appears thus in the source.] The poet said [in the kāmil metre; this is the eighth evidentiary verse]:
ذاكم وَجَدِّكُم الصَّغار بأسرِه * لا أُمَّ لي إنْ كان ذاكَ ولا أَبُ
(That, by your fortune, is utter humiliation; may I have no mother and no father if that should be.)
So he made one of them nominative and the other accusative.
As for His words ﴿لاَ فِيهَا غَوْلٌ﴾, it is nominative because "لا" is [not] strong enough to govern when it is separated [from its noun], and you have separated it by "فيها"; so it is nominative as a mubtadaʾ, and "لا" does not govern.
His words ﴿فِيهِ هُدًى لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾: ["فيه"], "عليه", "إليه" and the like are frequent in the Quran. That is because, when this masculine hāʾ is preceded by a vowelless yāʾ, the Arabs drop the yāʾ or wāw that comes after the hāʾ, because the hāʾ is a faint letter that has fallen between two similar letters, and that is heavy. So whoever, in his dialect, adds the wāw when a kasra precedes [the hāʾ] and no yāʾ precedes it, leaves the hāʾ with ḍamma when a vowelless yāʾ precedes it; and whoever, in his dialect, adds the wāw when a kasra precedes it and no yāʾ precedes it, leaves the hāʾ with ḍamma when a vowelless yāʾ precedes it [Translator's note: this sentence is repeated in the source]; and whoever, in his dialect, adds the yāʾ leaves the hāʾ with kasra when a vowelless yāʾ precedes it. Likewise, when the hāʾ is preceded by a vowelless alif or a wāw, he drops the wāw that comes after the hāʾ, but the hāʾ can only have ḍamma, as in ﴿فَأَلْقَىٰ مُوسَىٰ عَصَاهُ﴾, His words ﴿فَكَذَّبُوهُ﴾ and His words ﴿فَأَنجَيْنَاهُ﴾; there is much like this in the Quran.
Some Arabs pronounce it in full, because that is the original, saying ﴿فكذّبُوهو﴾, ﴿فأنجَيْناهو﴾, ﴿وألقى موسى عصاهو﴾ and ﴿لا ريبَ فيهُو هُدىً للمتقين﴾; this is the reading of the people of Medina. Some people said ﴿إِنِّي لَكُمْ مِّنْهُ نَذِيرٌ مُّبِينٌ﴾, dropping the wāw and likening the vowelless letter to yāʾ, wāw and alif. This is not good in Arabic; the best is ﴿منهو نذير﴾, with the wāw added even though it is not written. In all of this, when you pause on it, you add nothing to the hāʾ.
This hāʾ is given kasra only when a vowelless yāʾ or a letter with kasra precedes it, and only the Banū Tamīm give it kasra. The people of the Hijaz give it ḍamma after kasra and after yāʾ as well. He said ﴿ثُمَّ ٱتَّخَذْتُمُ ٱلْعِجْلَ مِن بَعْدِهِ وَأَنْتُمْ ظَالِمُونَ﴾, and the people of the Hijaz [say] ﴿من بعدِهُو﴾, keeping the wāw in every position.
Some Arabs drop the wāw and the yāʾ in cases of this kind too; that is rare and ugly. He says "مررت بِهِ قبلُ" and "بِهُ قبلُ" (I passed by him before), with kasra and with ḍamma, adding neither wāw nor yāʾ, and they say "رأيتُهُ قبلُ" (I saw him before) without adding a wāw. We have heard some of that from eloquent Arabs.
Some Quran readers read ﴿فِيهْ هُدَى﴾, assimilating the first hāʾ * into the hāʾ of ﴿هُدى﴾, because they met and are identical. [Translator's note: the asterisk appears thus in the source.]
They claimed that some Arabs treat "الهُدى" (guidance) as feminine. Some of them make the masculine pronoun hāʾ vowelless; the poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; this is the ninth evidentiary verse]:
فَظِلْتُ لدى البيت العتيق أُخيلُه * ومِطواي مشتاقانِ لَهْ أرِقانِ
(I stayed by the Ancient House watching it [for lightning], and my two companions were longing for it and sleepless.)
This is frequent, they claimed, in the dialect of Asad al-Sarāt.

akhfash:3-3.t:
His words ﴿وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ يُنْفِقُونَ﴾: there are two dialect forms in it. Some say it with pause [i.e. vowelless mīm] when connecting, and some add a wāw in it. It is like this in every place in the Quran and in speech, unless what precedes it has kasra or is a vowelless yāʾ. If it is a vowelless yāʾ or a letter with kasra, as in "عليْهِم", "بِهِمْ" and "مِن بعدِهِمْ", then some Arabs say "عليهِمِي", adding the yāʾ and giving kasra to the mīm and the hāʾ; some say "عليْهُمُو", adding the wāw and giving ḍamma to the mīm and the hāʾ; some say "عليهِم" and "عليهُم", giving the hāʾ ḍamma or kasra and making the mīm vowelless; some say "عليهِمُو", giving the hāʾ kasra, the mīm ḍamma and adding the wāw; and some say "عليهُمِي", giving the hāʾ ḍamma, the mīm kasra and adding the yāʾ.
In all of this, when you pause on it, its last letter is vowelless; and what is preceded by a kasra is treated like what is preceded by a yāʾ. This is frequent in the Quran.
Some treat ["كُمْ] in] "عليكم" and "بكم", when preceded by a vowelless yāʾ or a letter with kasra, like "هُمْ". That is ugly and hardly known; it is a dialect of Bakr ibn Wāʾil. We heard it from some of them, saying "عليكِمي" and "بِكِمي". Al-Akhfash recited, saying he heard it from Bakr ibn Wāʾil [in the ṭawīl metre; this is the tenth evidentiary verse]:
وإنْ قالَ مولاهمْ على جُلِّ حاجةٍ * من الأمرِ رُدّوا فَضْلَ أحلامِكِم رَدُّوا
(If their kinsman says, in some grave matter of need, "Bring back the surplus of your forbearance", they bring it back.)
In all of this, when a vowelless letter meets it, the mīm is given ḍamma if a wāw follows it; if a wāw follows it, the wāw is dropped; and if [it is] a yāʾ, the yāʾ is dropped and the mīm is given kasra. [Translator's note: so in the source; the sense is that the mīm takes the vowel of the dropped wāw or yāʾ.]
The same applies to the hāʾ for the masculine singular, as in "مررت به اليوم" (I passed by him today) and "رأيته اليوم" (I saw him today).
They claimed that some Arabs give the mīm a vowel without adding yāʾ or wāw in poetry, and this is hardly known. The poet said [in the rajaz metre; this is the eleventh evidentiary verse]:
تاللهِ لولا شُعْبتي من الكرم * وشعبتي فيهِم من خالٍ وعَمّ
(By Allah, were it not for my share of nobility, and my share among them of maternal and paternal uncles…)

akhfash:119-119.t: He said: ﴿إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ بِٱلْحَقِّ بَشِيراً وَنَذِيراً وَلاَ تُسْأَلُ عَنْ أَصْحَابِ ٱلْجَحِيمِ﴾. It has also been read ﴿ولا تَسْأَلُ﴾. All of this is nominative (marfūʿ), because it is not a prohibition; it is only a ḥāl (circumstantial), as though He had said: "We sent you as a bearer of good tidings and a warner, and not asking" or "not being asked" ("غيرَ سائِلٍ أو غيرَ مَسؤْول"). Both have also been read in the jussive (majzūm), as a prohibition.

akhfash:121-121.t: He said: ﴿يَتْلُونَهُ حَقَّ تِلاَوَتِهِ﴾, as they say "هذا حَقٌّ عالمٍ" ("this is truly a scholar"), and it is like "هذا عالِمٌ كُلُّ عالِمٍ" ("this is a scholar, every bit a scholar").

akhfash:40-40.t:
As for His saying ﴿يَابَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ﴾: among the Arabs there are those who pronounce it with a hamza and those who do not. And among them are those who say ﴿إسرَائِل﴾, dropping the yāʾ that comes after the hamza, and pronouncing the hamza with a fatḥa or with a kasra.
Chapter on the conditional (al-mujāzāh).
As for His saying ﴿وَأَوْفُواْ بِعَهْدِيۤ أُوفِ بِعَهْدِكُمْ﴾: the second verb is jussive (majzūm) only because it is the answer to the command, and the answer to a command is jussive just like the answer to what follows the conditional particles. It is as though it were the interpretation of "if you do [so]", I shall fulfil My covenant with you. And He said in another place ﴿ذَرُونَا نَتَّبِعْكُمْ﴾, and He said ﴿فَذَرْهُمْ فِي خَوْضِهِمْ يَلْعَبُونَ﴾, and He did not make it an answer; rather, it is as though they were [already] playing, so He said, "leave them in the state of their playing". And He said ﴿ذَرْهُمْ يَأْكُلُواْ وَيَتَمَتَّعُواْ وَيُلْهِهِمُ ٱلأَمَلُ﴾, and that does not come about because of the leaving; rather, Allah knew that it would be, and it ran according to the grammatical inflection as though He had said: "If you leave them, hope will divert them", while they are like that whether He leaves them or not. Just as some speech has a known wording while the meaning is otherwise, and just as some of them say: "كَذَبَ عليكُمُ الحجّ" (literally "the pilgrimage has lied to you").
So "الحجُّ" is nominative (marfūʿ), while they only intend to command [people] to [perform] the pilgrimage. The poet said [in the kāmil metre; it is the forty-eighth shāhid (evidentiary verse)]:
كَذَبَ العتيقُ وماءُ شنٍّ باردٍ * إن كنتِ سائِلتي غَبوقاً فاذْهَبي
(Keep to the old date-wine [lit. "the old wine has lied"] and the cool water of a skin; if you are asking me for an evening drink [of milk], then go away.)
And he said [in the wāfir metre; it is the forty-ninth shāhid]:
وذُبْيانِية توصي بينها * أَلا كَذَبَ القراطِفُ والقُروفُ
(And a woman of Dhubyān advising her sons: "Make sure of the velvet cloaks and the leather food-bags.")
Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: "القَراطِفُ": its singular is "قَرْطَفٌ", which is any garment that has a pile. And "القُروفُ": its singular is "قَرْفٌ", which is a container made of camel hides in which they used to boil meat and carry it on their journeys. And they say "هذا جُحرُ ضبٍّ خَرِبٍ" ("this is the hole of a lizard, ruined"), while the one that is ruined is the hole. And they say [one of them]: "هذا حبُّ رُمّاني" ("these are the seeds of my pomegranates"), so he annexes the pomegranates to himself, while only the seeds are his. This is frequent in speech.
And His saying ﴿قُل لِّلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ يَغْفِرُواْ لِلَّذِينَ لاَ يَرْجُونَ أَيَّامَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ and ﴿وَقُل لِّعِبَادِي يَقُولُواْ ٱلَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ﴾: He ran it according to the wording, so that it became an answer to the command. Some people have claimed that this is only on [the reading of] "فَلْيَغْفِروا" and "قُلْ لَعِبادي فَليَقولوا"; but all of this is not implied, meaning the fāʾ and the lām. If this were permissible, it would [be] permissible for a man to say "يَقُمْ زَيْدٌ" meaning "لَيَقُمْ زَيْدٌ" ("let Zayd stand"). And this phrase [of yours] is also more acceptable, because you have not implied in it the fāʾ together with the lām.
And they have claimed that the lām has come implied. The poet said [in the wāfir metre; it is the fiftieth shāhid]:
مُحَمَّدُ تَفْد نَفْسَكَ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ * إذا ما خِفْتَ من شَيْءٍ تَبالا
(Muḥammad, may every soul ransom your soul, whenever you fear the evil consequence of something.)
He means "لِتَفْدِ", and this is ugly (qabīḥ). And he said: "تَقِ اللّهَ امرُؤٌ فعل كذا وكذا" ("let a man fear Allah who did such-and-such"), and its meaning is "ليَتَّق اللّهَ". For the wording frequently comes differing from the meaning, and this indicates it. The poet said, regarding the implied lām [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the fifty-first shāhid]:
على مثلِ أصحاب البعوضَةِ فَاخمِشي * لكِ الويلُ حُرَّ الوَجْهِ أو يَبْكِ من بكى
(Over the like of the men of al-Baʿūḍa scratch — woe to you — the fair skin of your face, or let whoever weeps weep.)
He means "ليبكِ مَنْ بكى", and he omitted [the lām]. And I heard among the Arabs one who recites this verse without a lām [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the fifty-second shāhid]:
فَيَبْكِ على المِنْجابِ أضيافُ قَفْرةٍ * سَرَوْا وأُسارى لم تُفَكَّ قيودُها
(So let the guests of the wasteland who travelled by night weep for al-Minjāb, and captives whose fetters have not been loosed.)
He means "فَلْيَبْكِ", and he omitted the lām.
Chapter on the explanation of أنا, أنت and هو
Chapter on the explanation of أنا, أنت and هو.
As for His saying ﴿وَإِيَّايَ فَٱرْهَبُونِ﴾ [and] ﴿وَإِيَّايَ فَٱتَّقُونِ﴾: He said ﴿وَإيّايَ﴾ although you have occupied the verb with the pronoun that comes after the verb. This is because everything of this kind involving command and prohibition is accusative (manṣūb), as in your saying: "زيداً فَاضْرِبْ أَخاهُ" ("Zayd — strike his brother"). For command and prohibition are among the things in which [a verb] is often implied, and implication is good in them. The nominative is also permissible, on the basis of not implying [a verb]. The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the fifty-third shāhid]:
وقائِلَةٍ خولانَ فانكَحْ فتاتَهُمْ * وأُكْرومَةُ الحَيَّيْنِ خِلّوُكما هِيا
(Many a woman saying: "Khawlān — marry their maiden!", while the noblest girl of the two clans is unmarried as she is.)
[Translator's note: the second half-verse is printed here as «خِلّوُكما هِيا»; in its repetition later in this entry it appears as «خلوٌ كَما هِيا». Both are translated as written.]
As for His saying ﴿ٱلزَّانِيَةُ وَٱلزَّانِي فَٱجْلِدُواْ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ مِّنْهُمَا﴾ [and] ﴿وَٱلسَّارِقُ وَٱلسَّارِقَةُ فَٱقْطَعُوۤاْ أَيْدِيَهُمَا﴾: they have claimed — and Allah knows best — that this is on [the pattern of] the revelation, as though He were saying: "And among what I relate to you are the adulteress and the adulterer, and the thief, female and male". Then He brought the verb after He had made the first [noun] necessarily nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject). This is by way of figurative usage (majāz), as though He had said: "The matter of the thief, male and female, and their affair are among what We relate to you". Similar to it is His saying ﴿مَّثَلُ ٱلْجَنَّةِ ٱلَّتِي وُعِدَ ٱلْمُتَّقُونَ﴾, then He said ﴿فِيهَآ أَنْهَارٌ مِّن مَّآءٍ﴾, as though He had said: "And among what I relate to you is the description of the Garden", then He went on to mention what is in it, after He had made the first [noun] necessarily nominative as a mubtadaʾ. Some people have read them in the accusative, since the verb falls on something connected with the first [noun], and it is in [the context of] command and prohibition. Likewise what the interrogative particle falls on, as in His saying ﴿أَبَشَرَاً مِنّا واحِداً نَتَّبِعُه﴾. This was done with the interrogative particles only because, when a noun and a verb come after it, it is better to begin with the verb before the noun; so if you begin with the noun, you imply a verb for it so that the speech is made good by it, and making that verb overt is ugly.
Whatever of this kind is outside command, prohibition, interrogation and negation, the proper way of speech in it is the nominative; yet many people among the Arabs have put it in the accusative. And this word has been read both in the accusative and in the nominative: ﴿وَأَمَّا ثَمُودُ فَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ﴾.
As for His saying ﴿إِنَّا كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقْنَاهُ بِقَدَرٍ﴾: the nominative is permissible in it, and it is the more widespread usage, except that the community [of readers] agreed on the accusative; and they sometimes agree in this way on something that is permissible while the base is otherwise. For your saying "إنّا عَبدُ اللّهِ ضَرَبْناهُ" ("We — ʿAbd Allāh, we struck him") is like your saying "عبدُ اللّهِ ضَرَبْناهُ" ("ʿAbd Allāh, we struck him"), because their meaning with respect to the ibtidāʾ (inchoative position) is the same. The poet said [in the mutaqārib metre; it is the fifty-fourth shāhid]:
فأَمّا تَمِيمٌ تَميمُ بنُ مُرٍّ * فأَلْفاهُمُ القومُ رَوْبى نِياما
(As for Tamīm, Tamīm ibn Murr, the people found them heavy with sleep, sleeping.)
And he said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the fifty-fifth shāhid]:
إذا ابنُ أبي مُوسى بلالٌ بلغتِهِ * فقامَ بفأسٍ بينَ وَصْلَيكِ جازِرُ
(When you [my camel] have reached Ibn Abī Mūsā, Bilāl, then may a butcher stand with an axe between your two joints.)
And the accusative is possible in both of them. Whoever read ﴿وأَما ثَمُودَ﴾ in the accusative read it so on this basis.
As for His saying ﴿يُدْخِلُ مَن يَشَآءُ فِي رَحْمَتِهِ وَٱلظَّالِمِينَ أَعَدَّ لَهُمْ﴾, and His saying ﴿أَأَنتُمْ أَشَدُّ خَلْقاً أَمِ ٱلسَّمَآءُ بَنَاهَا﴾ then He said ﴿وَٱلأَرْضَ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ دَحَاهَا﴾, and He said ﴿ٱلرَّحْمَـٰنُ [1] عَلَّمَ ٱلْقُرْآنَ [2] خَلَقَ ٱلإِنسَانَ [3] عَلَّمَهُ ٱلبَيَانَ﴾ then He said ﴿وَٱلسَّمَآءَ رَفَعَهَا وَوَضَعَ ٱلْمِيزَانَ﴾, and He said ﴿وَكُلاًّ ضَرَبْنَا لَهُ ٱلأَمْثَالَ وَكُلاًّ تَبَّرْنَا تَتْبِيراً﴾: this is put in the accusative even though the verb has fallen on the noun after it [i.e. its pronoun], because the noun before it has been governed [by a verb], so you imply a verb and make it govern it, so that the government is of one kind. And that is better. [The poet] said [in the wāfir metre; it is the fifty-sixth shāhid]:
نغالي اللحمَ للأضيافِ نَيْئاً * ونُرْخِصُه إذا نَضِجَ القُدورَ
(We pay dearly for meat for the guests while it is raw, and we make it cheap [give it freely] when the pots are cooked.)
[Translator's note: «القُدورَ» is printed in the accusative as written.]
He means "نُغالي باللحم". And if you say [that] ﴿يُدْخِلُ مَن يَشَآءُ﴾ is not accusative in its wording, [the answer is that] it is in the position of the accusative, a verb having governed it, just as you say: "مررت بزيدٍ وعَمْراً ضربتُه" ("I passed by Zayd, and ʿAmr I struck him"), as though you had said "مررت زيداً". Some people actually say this. The poet said [in the munsariḥ metre; it is the fifty-seventh shāhid]:
أَصبحتُ لا أَحْمِلُ السلاحَ ولا * آمِلْكُ رأسَ البعيِرِ إنْ نَفَرا
والذيبَ أخشاهُ إنْ مَرَرْتُ بهِ * وَحدِي وأَخشى الرياحَ والمَطَرا
(I have become such that I cannot carry weapons, nor control the camel's head if it bolts; and the wolf I fear if I pass by it alone, and I fear the winds and the rain.)
All of this permits the nominative as a mubtadaʾ, but the accusative is better and more frequent.
As for His saying ﴿يَغْشَىٰ طَآئِفَةً مِّنْكُمْ وَطَآئِفَةٌ قَدْ أَهَمَّتْهُمْ أَنْفُسُهُمْ﴾: it is only on the basis of His saying "it overcomes a party of you, while [another] party is in this state". [And] this is a wāw of ibtidāʾ (a wāw beginning a new clause), not a wāw of conjunction, as you say: "ضربتُ عبْدَ اللّهِ وزيدٌ قائم" ("I struck ʿAbd Allāh while Zayd was standing"). It has also been read in the accusative, because it is like what we have mentioned; that is because the verb may fall on something connected with it while what precedes it is accusative by a verb, so you conjoin it to it and imply a verb for it and put it in the accusative by it. And what we mentioned in this chapter of His saying ﴿وَٱلسَّارِقُ وَٱلسَّارِقَةُ فَٱقْطَعُوۤاْ أَيْدِيَهُمَا﴾ [and His saying] ﴿ٱلزَّانِيَةُ وَٱلزَّانِي فَٱجْلِدُواْ﴾: in His saying ﴿فَٱقْطَعُوۤاْ﴾ and ﴿فَٱجْلِدُواْ﴾ there is no khabar (predicate) of a mubtadaʾ, because the khabar of a mubtadaʾ is not like this, with the fāʾ. [So] if you said "عبدُ اللّهِ فَيَنْطَلِقُ" it would not be good. The khabar is only the implied one that I explained to you, namely His saying "and among what We relate to you". And it is like his saying [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the fifty-third shāhid]:
وقائلةٍ خولانُ فانكحْ فتاتَهُم * [وأكرومةُ الحَيَّيْنِ خلوٌ كَما هِيا]
(Many a woman saying: "[These are] Khawlān — marry their maiden!" [while the noblest girl of the two clans is unmarried as she is].)
As though he had said: "These are Khawlān", just as you say: "الهلالُ فانظرْ اليهِ" ("the new moon — look at it"), as though you had said: "This is the new moon, so look at it", and he implied the noun.
As for His saying ﴿وَٱللَّذَانِ يَأْتِيَانِهَا مِنكُمْ فَآذُوهُمَا﴾: this may be the khabar of the mubtadaʾ, because "الذي", when its ṣila (relative clause) is a verb, may have its khabar with the fāʾ, as in the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic ﴿إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ تَوَفَّاهُمُ ٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةُ ظَالِمِيۤ أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾, then He said ﴿فَأُوْلَـٰئِكَ مَأْوَاهُمْ جَهَنَّمُ﴾.

akhfash:124-124.t:
He said: ﴿وَإِذِ ٱبْتَلَىٰ إِبْرَاهِيمَ رَبُّهُ بِكَلِمَاتٍ﴾, that is: He tested him. And ﴿إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ is the one tested, which is why it is accusative.
And He said: ﴿لاَ يَنَالُ عَهْدِي ٱلظَّالِمِينَ﴾, because the covenant is what does not reach them. Some read ﴿لا ينالُ عهدي الظالِمُون﴾, while the written text (the muṣḥaf) has it with yāʾ. They read ﴿الظالمونَ﴾ only because they made them the ones who do not attain.

akhfash:45-45.t:
Chapter on the wāw.
As for His saying ﴿وَٱسْتَعِينُواْ بِٱلصَّبْرِ وَٱلصَّلاَةِ وَإِنَّهَا لَكَبِيرَةٌ﴾: it is because He made the speech refer to "the prayer". This is speech of which some is made to refer to the first [item] and some to the last. And He said ﴿وَٱللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ أَحَقُّ أَن يُرْضُوهُ﴾, and this is permissible [as referring] to the first and to the last; and the more analogical (aqyas) course, when it is with the wāw, is to make it refer to both of them together. You say: "زيد وعمرو ذاهبان" ("Zayd and ʿAmr are going"). This is not like "أو", because with "أو" one only gives information about one of the two things. With "أو" you have the choice: if you wish, you make the speech refer to the first, and if you wish, to the last; and making it refer to the last is more analogical, because making the khabar (predicate) refer to the noun that is next to it [the khabar] is better than passing over it to a noun far from it. He said ﴿وَإِذَا رَأَوْاْ تِجَارَةً أَوْ لَهْواً ٱنفَضُّوۤاْ إِلَيْهَا﴾, and He made it refer to the first; and He said in another place ﴿وَمِن رَّحْمَتِهِ جَعَلَ لَكُمُ ٱلْلَّيْلَ وَٱلنَّهَارَ لِتَسْكُنُواْ فِيهِ﴾, and He said ﴿وَمَن يَكْسِبْ خَطِيۤئَةً أَوْ إِثْماً ثُمَّ يَرْمِ بِهِ بَرِيئاً﴾, and He made it refer to the last. The poet said [in the basīṭ metre; it is the fifty-eighth shāhid (evidentiary verse)]:
أمّا الوَسامَةُ أو حُسْنُ النِساءِ فَقَدْ * أُوتيتِ مِنْهُ لو انَّ العقلَ محتَنِكُ
(As for comeliness or the beauty of women, you have been given [much] of it — if only your reason were mature.)
And Ibn Aḥmar said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the fifty-ninth shāhid]:
رماني بداءٍ كنتُ منهُ ووالدي * بريئاً ومن أَجْلِ الطَوِيِّ رماني
(He charged me with an evil of which I and my father were innocent, and on account of the well he charged me.)
And the other said [in the munsariḥ metre; it is the sixtieth shāhid]:
نحنُ بِما عندَنا وأنتَ بما * عندَكَ راضٍ والرأيُ مُخْتَلِفُ
(We with what we have, and you with what you have, are content, and opinion differs.)
And this is like the saying of al-Burjumī [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the sixty-first shāhid]:
مَنْ يكُ أمْسى بالمدينةِ دارُهُ * فإنّي وَقَيّاراً بِها لَغَرِيبُ
(Whoever has come to have his home in Medina — I and Qayyār are strangers in it.)
As for His saying ﴿بِٱتِّخَاذِكُمُ ٱلْعِجْلَ فَتُوبُوۤاْ إِلَىٰ بَارِئِكُمْ﴾:
﴿ٱلْعِجْلَ﴾ is accusative (manṣūb) because it is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object); you say: "عجبت من ضربِكَ زيداً" ("I was amazed at your striking Zayd"). And His saying ﴿بَارِئِكُمْ﴾ has a hamza because it is from "برأ اللّهُ الخلقَ" ("Allah created the creation"), "يَبْرأُ", "بَرْءاً". Some of them have read this hamza with lightening (takhfīf), making it between a hamza and a yāʾ. Some people have claimed that it is made jussive [i.e. given sukūn], and I consider that nothing but a mistake on their part: they heard the lightening and thought that it was jussive, while lightening is only understood by oral transmission and is not known in writing. Giving it sukūn is not permissible, unless he gave it sukūn and treated it like "عَلْمَ", "قَدْ ضُرْبَ", "قَدْ سَمْعَ" and the like.
I heard among the Arabs one who says: ﴿جَآءَتْ رُسُلْنا﴾, giving the lām sukūn, and that is because of the abundance of vowels. The poet said [in the sarīʿ metre; it is the seventy-second shāhid]:
[Translator's note: the numbering jumps here from the sixty-first to the seventy-second shāhid; the numbers are reproduced as written.]
وأنتِ لو باكرتِ مَشْمولَةً * صهباءَ مثلَ الفَرَسِ الأشْقَرِ
رُحْتِ وفي رجلَيكِ ما فيهما * وقد بَداهَنْكِ من المِئزِرِ
(And you, had you started the morning with cool wine, reddish like a sorrel horse, you would have gone off with your legs [unsteady] as they are, and your private part would have shown from under the waist-wrapper.)
And Imruʾ al-Qays said [in the sarīʿ metre; it is the seventy-third shāhid]:
فاليومَ أشربْ غيرَ مُستحقبٍ * إِثماً من اللّهِ ولا واغِلِ
(So today I drink, not burdening myself with a sin before Allah, nor as an uninvited guest.)
And another said [in the rajaz metre; it is the seventy-fourth shāhid]:
* إنَّ بَنِي ثَمَرَةْ فُؤادي *
(My sons are the fruit of my heart.)
And another said [in the rajaz metre; it is the seventy-fifth shāhid]:
يا عَلْقَمة يا عَلْقَمة يا علقمة * خيرَ تميمٍ كلِّها وأَكرمَهْ
(O ʿAlqama, O ʿAlqama, O ʿAlqama, best of all Tamīm and the most noble of it.)
And he said [in the rajaz metre; it is the seventy-sixth shāhid]:
إذا اعوججْنَ صاحبْ قَوِّمِ * بالدَّوِّ أمثالَ السفينِ العُوَّمِ
(When they [the camels] veer, comrade, set straight, in the open desert, [beasts] like floating ships.)
And "رُسُلْنا" may be by assimilation (idghām): he assimilates the lām into the nūn and gives it a nasalisation (ghunna). And the sukūn in ﴿بارئْكُم﴾ is by substitution [of the hamza], in the dialect of those who said "أَخْطَيْت"; and this is not known.

akhfash:125-125.t:
He said: ﴿وَإِذْ جَعَلْنَا ٱلْبَيْتَ مَثَابَةً لِّلنَّاسِ وَأَمْناً﴾, [conjoined] to ﴿ٱذْكُرُواْ نِعْمَتِي ٱلَّتِيۤ أَنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ ... ﴿وَإِذْ جَعَلْنَا ٱلْبَيْتَ مَثَابَةً لِّلنَّاسِ﴾. The hāʾ (the feminine ending) was attached to "المَثابة" because of the great number of those who return to it, just as you say "نَسَّابَة" (a great genealogist) and "سيّارَة" (a great traveller) of someone who does that a great deal.
And He said: ﴿وَٱتَّخِذُواْ مِن مَّقَامِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ مُصَلًّى﴾, meaning ﴿واتَّخَذُوا﴾ (past tense), as though He were saying: "And remember My favour, and when they took a place of prayer from the station of Ibrāhīm". [It is also read] ﴿اتخّذُوا﴾ with kasra, and that is how we read it, because it indicates the purpose.
And He said: ﴿وَٱلرُّكَّعِ ٱلسُّجُودِ﴾: ﴿ٱلسُّجُودِ﴾ is the plural of "السَّاجد" (one who prostrates), just as you say "قَوْمٌ قُعُودٌ" (people sitting) and "جُلوسٌ" (seated).

akhfash:46-46.t:
Chapter on the active participle (ism al-fāʿil).
He said ﴿ٱلَّذِينَ يَظُنُّونَ أَنَّهُم مُّلاَقُو رَبِّهِمْ﴾: He used annexation (iḍāfa) in His saying ﴿مُّلاَقُو رَبِّهِمْ﴾ although the action has not taken place. Annexation is only used when the action has taken place: you say "هم ضاربوا ابيك" ("they are the strikers of your father") when they have struck him; and when they are in the course of striking, or have not struck, you say "هم ضاربون أخاك" ("they are striking your brother"). However, the Arabs sometimes find the nūn heavy and drop it while meaning its retention, and that is like ﴿مُّلاَقُو رَبِّهِمْ﴾, like ﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ذَآئِقَةُ ٱلْمَوْتِ﴾ when it has not yet tasted [it]. Some of them have said: ﴿ذائقةٌ الموتَ﴾, according to what I have explained to you. And Allah, exalted be His praise, said ﴿إِنَّا مُرْسِلُو ٱلنَّاقَةِ﴾, and this was before the sending, but the nūn was dropped out of a sense of heaviness. And He said ﴿وَكَلْبُهُمْ بَاسِطٌ ذِرَاعَيْهِ﴾, and kept the tanwīn because it was in the present. And He said ﴿إِنَّا كَاشِفُو ٱلْعَذَابِ قَلِيلاً﴾ on that basis too. And they have claimed that this verse is recited thus [in the basīṭ metre; it is the sixty-second shāhid (evidentiary verse)]:
هل أنتَ باعثُ دينارٍ لحاجَتِنا‌ * او عبد ربٍّ أخا عمرو بنِ مِخْراقِ
(Will you send Dīnār for our need, or ʿAbd Rabb, the brother of ʿAmr ibn Mikhrāq?)
He used annexation although the action had not taken place, and put the second in the accusative according to the meaning, because the first has the intention of the tanwīn, like the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿وَجَعَلَ ٱلْلَّيْلَ سَكَناً وَٱلشَّمْسَ وَٱلْقَمَرَ حُسْبَاناً﴾. If you put "the sun", "the moon" and "ʿAbd Rabb, the brother of ʿAmr" in the genitive, conjoined to what you put the first in the genitive with, it would be permissible and good. And He said ﴿إِنَّا مُنَجُّوكَ وَأَهْلَكَ إِلاَّ ٱمْرَأَتَكَ﴾: the accusative is the proper way of speech, because you do not conjoin an overt noun to a [genitive] pronoun, and the kāf is in the position of the genitive because of the disappearance of the nūn. That is because when this [participle] falls on a pronoun, the tanwīn and the nūn disappear from it, even if it is in the present and he has not done [the action]. You say: "هو ضاربُك الساعةَ أو غداً" ("he is striking you now or tomorrow") and "هم ضاربوك". And when you add the alif and lām, you say "هو الضارب زيداً" ("he is the one striking Zayd"), and it cannot be that you put "زيداً" in the genitive, because the tanwīn is as if still present in "الضارب" when it has the alif and lām, since the alif and lām alternate with the tanwīn. And you say "هما الضاربانِ زيداً" and "هما الضاربا زيدٍ", because the alif and lām do not alternate with the tanwīn in the dual and the plural. So when you remove the nūn from the dual and the plural of active participles, you annex, even if it has the alif and lām, because the nūn alternates with annexation; and dropping the nūn here is like dropping the nūn in your saying "هما ضاربا زيد" when they have not done [it], because the base in your saying "الضاربان" is retention of the nūn, since its meaning and its governing are like the meaning and governing of "الذي فعل" ("the one who did"). The poet said [in the munsariḥ metre; it is the sixty-third shāhid]:
الحافظو عورةِ العشيرِ لا * يأتيُهمُ من ورائِنا نطف
(Those who guard the weak spot of the clan — no blemish comes to them from behind us.)
And in the Book of Allah there is ﴿وَٱلْمُقِيمِي ٱلصَّلاَةِ﴾; and some of them read it in the accusative, saying ﴿وَٱلْمُقِيمِي ٱلصَّلاةَ﴾, and "الحافظو عورةَ", out of a sense of the heaviness of annexation, just as the nūn of "اللَذينِ" and "الذينَ" was dropped. The poet said [in the kāmil metre; it is the sixty-fourth shāhid]:
أَبَنِي كُلَيْبٍ إنَّ عَمَّيَّ اللَذا * قَتَلا المُلوكَ وَفَكَّكا الأغْلالا
(O sons of Kulayb, my two uncles are the ones who killed kings and broke open the shackles.)
And he said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the sixty-fifth shāhid]:
فإنّ الذي حانَتْ بفَلْجٍ دماؤُهم * همُ القومُ كلُّ القومِ يا أُمَّ خالد
(Those whose blood was shed in vain at Falj are the people, all the people, O Umm Khālid.)
So he dropped the nūn. And they have claimed that ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar used to permit [in the mutaqārib metre; it is the sixty-sixth shāhid]:
فألفيتُهُ غيرَ مُستَعْتِبٍ * ولا ذاكِرَ اللّهَ الاّ قليلا
(I found him not seeking to make amends, nor remembering Allah except a little.)
It is as though he dropped the tanwīn not because of alternation with annexation; and that is ugly (qabīḥ), except in everything whose meaning is "اللذين" and "الذين", for then there is dropped from it what is dropped from those. If this verse were permissible, you would say "هم ضاربو زيدا", and this is not good. And they have claimed that one of the Arabs said ﴿وَٱعْلَمُوۤاْ أَنَّكُمْ غَيْرُ مُعْجِزِي ٱللَّهِ﴾ [Translator's note: i.e. with «ٱللَّهَ» in the accusative, as the context implies; the vowelling printed here shows the genitive], and he was Abū al-Sammāl, and he was eloquent. And this word has been read ﴿إِنَّكُمْ لَذَآئِقُو ٱلْعَذَابَ ٱلأَلِيمِ﴾, and it is more acceptable than [what is in] the verse, because he dropped the tanwīn [nūn] because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. And when you attach the nūn, you put [the object] in the accusative because the annexation has gone. He said ﴿وَٱلْمُقِيمِينَ ٱلصَّلاَةَ وَٱلْمُؤْتُونَ ٱلزَّكَاةَ﴾ [and] He said ﴿وَٱلذَّاكِـرِينَ ٱللَّهَ كَثِيراً﴾. The poet said [in the kāmil metre; it is the sixty-seventh shāhid]:
النازلونَ بكلِّ معتَرَكِ * والطيبونُ معاقدَ الأُزْرِ
(Those who alight at every battlefield, and those pure at the knots of the waist-wrappers [i.e. chaste].)

akhfash:126-126.t:
He said: ﴿وَٱرْزُقْ أَهْلَهُ مِنَ ٱلثَّمَرَاتِ مَنْ آمَنَ مِنْهُمْ﴾: ﴿مَنْ آمَنَ﴾ is a badal (substitute) by way of clarification, just as you say "أَخَذْتُ المالَ نِصْفَهُ" ("I took the money, half of it") and "رأيتُ القومَ ناساً مِنْهُم" ("I saw the people, some of them"). Similar to that is ﴿يَسْئَلُونَكِ عَنِ ٱلشَّهْرِ ٱلْحَرَامِ قِتَالٍ فِيهِ﴾, meaning "about fighting in it", and He made it a badal. Like it is ﴿وَللَّهِ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ حِجُّ ٱلْبَيْتِ مَنِ ٱسْتَطَاعَ إِلَيْهِ سَبِيلاً﴾, and like it ﴿قَالَ ٱلْمَلأُ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱسْتَكْبَرُواْ مِن قَوْمِهِ لِلَّذِينَ ٱسْتُضْعِفُواْ لِمَنْ آمَنَ مِنْهُمْ﴾ is also similar to this, except that the preposition is repeated in it. [Translator's note: the Arabic has «قدر فيه حرف الجرّ», literally "the preposition is estimated/set in it"; in the verse the preposition لِ is overtly repeated.]
And He said: ﴿وَمَن كَفَرَ فَأُمَتِّعُهُ قَلِيلاً﴾ — [some read it] as an imperative — ﴿ثُمَّ أَضْطَرُّهُ﴾: they put ﴿فَأَمْتِعْهُ﴾ in the jussive as an imperative and made the fāʾ the answer of the conditional (jawāb al-mujāzāt). Others read ﴿فَأُمَتِّعُهُ﴾, and that is how we read it: nominative as a statement, with the fāʾ as the answer of the conditional.

akhfash:127-127.t: He said: ﴿وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ ٱلْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ ٱلْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَاعِيلُ رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّآ﴾, that is: Ismāʿīl was the one who said ﴿رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّآ﴾.

akhfash:128-128.t: He said: ﴿وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَا﴾. Some read ﴿وأَرْنا﴾, making the rāʾ quiescent, just as you say "قَدْ عَلْمَ ذلك" (for عَلِمَ), but we read it with kasra. The singular of "المناسِك" (rites) is "مَنْسِك", like "مَسْجِد"; "مَنْسَك" is also said.

akhfash:130-130.t:
He said: ﴿إِلاَّ مَن سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾. The exegetes (ahl al-taʾwīl) claimed that it has the meaning of "سَفَّهَ نفسَه" ("he made a fool of himself"). Yūnus said: "I consider it a dialect usage." According to this view "سِفِهْتُ زَيْداً" is permissible, and it resembles "غِبَنَ رأيَه" ("he was deceived in his judgement") and "خَسِرَ نَفْسَه" ("he lost himself"), except that this [latter] is frequent, and this one has a meaning which that one does not. You say "غِبَنَ فيَ رأيِهِ", "خَسِرَ في أَهْلِهِ" and "خَسِرَ في بيعِه". There is a parallel for this: [one] said "ضُرِبَ عبدُ اللّهِ الظهرَ والبَطْنَ" ("ʿAbd Allāh was struck the back and the belly"), meaning "on the back and the belly", just as they said "دَخَلْتُ البيتَ" ("I entered the house"), when it is really "دَخَلْتُ في البيتِ" ("I entered into the house"); and the saying "تَوَجَّهَ مَكَّةَ والكُوفَةَ" ("he headed Mecca and Kufa"), when it is really "to Mecca and Kufa". Among what resembles this is the poet's saying [in the wāfir metre; it is the fifty-sixth shāhid (attested verse)]:
‌نُغالِي اللَّحْمَ لِلأَضْيافِ نِيْئاً * وَنَبْذُلُهُ إذا نَضِجَ القُدورُ
(We pay dearly for the meat for our guests while it is raw, and give it away freely when the pots have cooked.)
He means "نُغالى باللحم" (we pay dearly for the meat). Like this is ﴿وَإِنْ أَرَدتُّمْ أَن تَسْتَرْضِعُوۤاْ أَوْلاَدَكُمْ﴾; He is saying "for your children" ("لأوْلادِكمُ"); [and] ﴿وَلاَ تَعْزِمُوۤاْ عُقْدَةَ ٱلنِّكَاحِ﴾, that is: "upon the marriage tie" ("عَلَى عُقْدَةِ النِكاحِ"). Better [than] that is to say that "سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ" has been treated like "سَفُهَ", since the verb is intransitive, and it was only made to pass on to "نَفْسِه", "رَأيِهِ" and the like among what is in meaning like "سَفِهَ" when it is intransitive. As for "غَبِنَ" and "خَسِرَ", they can pass on to something else: you say "غَبِنَ خَمْسين" ("he was cheated of fifty") and "خَسِرَ خَمْسِين" ("he lost fifty").

akhfash:132-132.t: He said: ﴿وَوَصَّىٰ بِهَآ إِبْرَاهِيمُ بَنِيهِ وَيَعْقُوبُ يَابَنِيَّ﴾. It is — and Allah knows best — "and Yaʿqūb said: O my sons", because when He said ﴿وَوَصَّىٰ بِهَآ﴾ He had already informed us that he said something to them, so He made the latter run according to the meaning of the former. If you wish, you may say that ﴿وَيَعْقُوبُ﴾ is maʿṭūf (conjoined), as though you had said: "And Ibrāhīm enjoined it upon his sons, and Yaʿqūb [too]", and then He explained what Yaʿqūb said: he said "O my sons".

akhfash:133-133.t:
He said: ﴿أَمْ كُنتُمْ شُهَدَآءَ﴾: a resumptive (mustaʾnaf) question.
And He said: ﴿إِذْ حَضَرَ يَعْقُوبَ ٱلْمَوْتُ إِذْ قَالَ لِبَنِيهِ﴾: He made the second "إذْ" a badal (substitute) of the first.
And He said: ﴿إِلَـٰهَكَ وَإِلَـٰهَ آبَائِكَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ﴾ as a badal; it is in the position of the genitive, except that these are foreign names and so are diptotes.
And His saying ﴿إِلَـٰهاً وَاحِداً﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial).

akhfash:134-134.t: He said: ﴿تِلْكَ أُمَّةٌ قَدْ خَلَتْ لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ﴾: He is saying "has passed away", then He began anew (istaʾnafa) and said: ﴿لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ﴾.

akhfash:135-135.t: He said: ﴿بَلْ مِلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ in the accusative.

akhfash:138-138.t: He said: ﴿صِبْغَةَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ in the accusative, because when they said to them ﴿كُونُواْ هُوداً﴾, it was as though it had been said to them: "Adopt this religion", and they said: "No, ﴿بَلْ مِلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾", that is: we follow the religion of Ibrāhīm. Then He made "الصِّبْغَةَ" a badal (substitute) of "المِلَّة" and said ﴿صِبْغَةَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ in the accusative. Or He may have meant: "Be people of a religion" ("كونوا أصحابَ مِلَّةٍ"), then omitted "أَصْحاب", just as He said ﴿وَلَـٰكِنَّ ٱلْبِرَّ مَنْ آمَنَ بِٱللَّهِ﴾, meaning "the righteousness of the one who believes in Allah". And al-ṣibgha is religion.

akhfash:139-139.t:
He said: ﴿أَتُحَآجُّونّا﴾ with a doubled [nūn], because they are two identical letters, so one was assimilated into the other; and the quiescent letter before them was tolerated because it is one of the soft letters (ḥurūf al-līn). The soft letters are yāʾ, wāw and alif when they are quiescent.
Some read ﴿أتُحاجُّوننا﴾ without assimilating, but with concealment (ikhfāʾ): they made the vowel of the first [nūn] light, while it is vowelled in the metrical pattern. This is in the dialect of those who say "هذِهِ مِئَةُ دِّرْهَمٍ", giving a trace of the ḍamma without pronouncing it fully; that is ikhfāʾ. This word has been read in that way: ﴿مَا لَكَ لاَ تَأْمَنَّا عَلَىٰ يُوسُفَ﴾, between assimilation and clear pronunciation. Like that is ﴿إِنِّي لَيَحْزُنُنِيۤ أَن تَذْهَبُواْ بِهِ﴾, and the like of this is plentiful; but assimilating it, so that the first becomes quiescent, is better.

akhfash:140-140.t: He said: ﴿أَمْ يَقُولُونَ إِنَّ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾. Some read ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ﴾, [conjoined] to ﴿قُلْ أَتُحاجّونَنا﴾ … ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ﴾. Whoever reads ﴿أَمْ يَقُولُونَ﴾ makes it a resumptive (mustaʾnaf) question, just as you say "إنَّها لإِبِلٌ" ("they are surely camels"), then you say "أَمْ شاءٌ" ("or rather sheep?").

akhfash:142-142.t: He said: ﴿وَإِن كَانَتْ لَكَبِيرَةً﴾, meaning "the qibla", and that is why it is feminine.

akhfash:145-145.t: He said: ﴿وَلَئِنْ أَتَيْتَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُواْ ٱلْكِتَابَ بِكُلِّ آيَةٍ مَّا تَبِعُواْ قِبْلَتَكَ﴾, because the meaning of His saying ﴿وَلَئِنْ أَتَيْتَ﴾ is "and if [lit. 'law'] you brought". Do you not see that you say "لَئِنْ جِئْتَنِي ما ضَرَبْتُكَ" ("if you come to me I will not strike you") with the meaning of "لَوْ", just as He said ﴿وَلَئِنْ أَرْسَلْنَا رِيحاً فَرَأَوْهُ مُصْفَرّاً لَّظَلُّواْ﴾, saying "and if [law] We sent a wind"? For the meaning of "لَئِنْ" is like the meaning of "لَوْ", because "لَوْ" [refers to what] has not happened, and likewise "لَئِنْ"; that is how the exegetes explain it. In terms of i'rab, its end leans on the oath, as though He had said: "By Allah, they would not follow", that is: they are not followers.

akhfash:147-147.t: He said: ﴿ٱلْحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ﴾ on [the basis of] an implied pronoun noun, but it was dispensed with because He had mentioned it, as though He had said: "It is the truth from your Lord" ("هُوَ الحَقُّ مِنْ رَبِّكَ").

akhfash:148-148.t: He said: ﴿وَلِكُلٍّ وِجْهَةٌ هُوَ مُوَلِّيهَا﴾, on [the meaning]: "and for every community there is a direction". Some people read ﴿وَلِكُلِّ وُجْهَةٍ﴾, not giving "كلّ" tanwīn. This cannot be, because you do not say "لِكُلِّ رَجُلٍ هُو ضارِبُه" ("for every man he is his striker"); rather you say "لِكُلِّ رَجُلٍ ضارِبٌ" ("for every man there is a striker"). If it were "هُوَ مُوَلٍّ" it would be [valid] speech. But "مُولِّيها" in the way he read it is not permissible.

akhfash:150-150.t:
And He said: ﴿لِئَلاَّ يَكُونَ لِلنَّاسِ عَلَيْكُمْ حُجَّةٌ إِلاَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ﴾. This has the meaning of "لكنّ" (but). Yūnus claimed that he heard an eloquent Bedouin saying "ما أشْتَكِي شَيْئاً إلاَّ خَيْراً" ("I complain of nothing but good"), that being when he was asked "How do you find yourself?". And "إلاّ" can stand in the place of the wāw (and), as in the poet's saying [in the kāmil metre; it is the one hundred and thirtieth shāhid]:
وأَرى لَها دَاراً بأَغْدِرَةِ السـ * ـيِدانِ لم يَدْرُسْ لَها رَسْمُ
إلاّ رَماداً هامِداً دَفَعَتْ * عَنْهُ الرياحَ خَوالِدٌ سُحْمُ
(And I see that she has an abode at the pools of al-Sīdān whose traces have not been effaced, and [also] dead ashes from which black, enduring hearth-stones have kept off the winds.)
He meant: I see that she has an abode and ashes. Some of the learned said that "those who did wrong" here are people of the Arabs who were Jews or Christians and used to argue against the Prophet ﷺ; as for the rest of the Arabs, they had no argument, and the argument of whoever argued was broken. Yet you say to someone whose argument is broken: "You have an argument against me, but it is broken; you argue without an argument, and your argument is weak."
And He said: ﴿وَلأُتِمَّ نِعْمَتِي عَلَيْكُمْ﴾. He is saying: "so that people may have no argument against you, and so that I may complete My favour upon you" — conjoined to the first statement.

akhfash:151-151.t: His saying ﴿كَمَآ أَرْسَلْنَا فِيكُمْ رَسُولاً مِّنْكُمْ يَتْلُواْ عَلَيْكُمْ آيَاتِنَا وَيُزَكِّيكُمْ وَيُعَلِّمُكُمُ ٱلْكِتَابَ وَٱلْحِكْمَةَ﴾ ﴿فَٱذْكُرُونِيۤ أَذْكُرْكُمْ﴾, that is: just as I did this, so remember Me.

akhfash:154-154.t: He said: ﴿وَلاَ تَقُولُواْ لِمَنْ يُقْتَلُ فِي سَبيلِ ٱللَّهِ أَمْوَاتٌ﴾, on [the meaning]: "and do not say: they are dead". And He said: ﴿وَلاَ تَحْسَبَنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ قُتِلُواْ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ أَمْوَاتاً﴾, accusative by "تَحْسَبُ" (you think); then He said ﴿بِلْ أَحْياءٌ﴾, that is: "rather they are alive". It cannot be that you make it depend on the verb, because had He said "rather, think them alive" He would have commanded them to doubt.

akhfash:158-158.t: He said: ﴿فَلاَ جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِ أَن يَطَّوَّفَ بِهِمَا﴾: "إطَّوَّفَ", "يَطَّوّفُ", which is from "تَطَوَّفَ". The tāʾ was assimilated into the ṭāʾ, and when it became quiescent an alif was placed before it so that it could be pronounced at the start. He said ﴿لاَ جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ only because that was disliked in the Jāhiliyya — in the Jāhiliyya — so He informed [them] that it is not disliked in His sight.

akhfash:161-161.t: He said: ﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ لَعْنَةُ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾, because He put "the curse" in a genitive construct (iḍāfa); then He said ﴿خَالِدِينَ فِيهَا﴾, accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial).

akhfash:165-165.t:
He said: ﴿وَلَوْ تَرَى ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوۤاْ إِذْ يَرَوْنَ ٱلْعَذَابَ إِنَّ ٱلْقُوَّةَ للَّهِ جَمِيعاً﴾: "إنَّ" has kasra as a fresh start (ibtidāʾ), since He said ﴿وَلَوْ تَرى﴾. Some read ﴿ولو يَرى الذين ظلموا اذْ يَرَوْنَ العذاب أن القوةَ لِلّهِ جَميعاً﴾, saying: "and if they saw that power belongs to Allah", that is: "if they knew", because they had not known the extent of the punishment they would witness, whereas the Prophet ﷺ had. [Translator's note: the Arabic sentence «وقد كان النبي ﷺ» appears incomplete; "had [known]" is supplied from the context.] So when He says ﴿وَلَوْ تَرى﴾, He is addressing only the Prophet ﷺ. If one gave "إنّ" kasra when He says ﴿وَلَوْ يَرى الذينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾, as a fresh start, that would be permissible: "if he saw" or "knew". And it can have a meaning that needs nothing with it: you say to a man "أما وَاللّهِ لَوْ تَعْلَم" ("By Allah, if only you knew!") and "لَوْ يَعْلَم" ("if only he knew!"). The poet said [in the khafīf metre; it is the one hundred and thirty-first shāhid]:
إنْ يَكُنْ طِبَّكِ الدَّلالُ فَلَوْفِي * سالِفِ الدَّهْرِ والسنينَ الخَوالِي
(If coquetry is your habit — then if only [it had been] in bygone times and the years now past!)
This has no apodosis (jawāb) except in the meaning. And he said [in the khafīf metre; it is the one hundred and thirty-second shāhid]:
فَبِحَظٍّ مِمَا تَعيشُ ولا تَذْ * هَبْ بِكَ التُّرهاتُ في الأَهْوالِ
(So with a share of what you live by — and let not idle fancies carry you off into perils.)
So he implied "فعيشي" ("then live"). Some read ﴿وَلَوْ تَرى﴾ and gave ﴿أَنَّ﴾ fatḥa as depending on ﴿تَرى﴾. That is not because the Prophet ﷺ did not know, but He wanted to make that known to the people, just as He said ﴿أَمْ يَقُولُونَ ٱفْتَرَاهُ﴾, to inform the people of their ignorance, and as He said ﴿أَلَمْ تَعْلَمْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَهُ مُلْكُ ٱلسَّمَاوَاتِ وَٱلأَرْضِ﴾.

akhfash:6-6.t:
As for His words ﴿سَوَآءٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ أَمْ لَمْ تُنْذِرْهُمْ لاَ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾, the interrogative particle entered it although it is not a question, because of the mention of "السواء" (being equal). For when one says in a question "أَزيدْ عندك أم عَمْرو" (is Zayd with you or ʿAmr?), asking which of the two is with you, the two are equal for him, and neither is more entitled to be asked about than the other. So when equalisation came in His words ﴿أَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ﴾, it resembled that question, since it resembled it in equalisation. Similar to it is ﴿سَوَآءٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أَسْتَغْفَرْتَ لَهُمْ أَمْ لَمْ تَسْتَغْفِرْ لَهُمْ﴾; but ﴿أَسْتَغْفَرْتَ﴾ is not lengthened, because the alif in it is a connecting alif (alif waṣl), since it is from "اسْتَغْفَر", "يَستغِفرُ", where the yāʾ of "يَفْعل" has fatḥa. As for (أَأَنْذرتهم), it has two alifs: the alif of ﴿أَنْذَرت﴾, which is disjunctive because one says "يُنْذِرُ" with the yāʾ having ḍamma; then the interrogative alif was put with it, therefore it was lengthened and the second of them lightened, because two hamzas do not meet. And He said ﴿أَفلاَ تُبْصِرُونَ﴾ ﴿أَمْ أَنَآ خَيْرٌ مِّنْ هَـٰذَا ٱلَّذِي هُوَ مَهِينٌ﴾. Some said it depends on His words ﴿أَفلاَ تُبْصِرُونَ﴾, and he made His words ﴿أَمْ أَنَآ خَيْرٌ مِّنْ هَـٰذَا ٱلَّذِي هُوَ مَهِينٌ﴾ a badal (substitute) for ﴿تُبْصِرُونَ﴾, because for him it would be insight on their part that it should be thus with them. This is the "أم" that has the sense of "أيهما" (which of the two). Some said: "It is Yemeni", because the people of Yemen add "أم" throughout speech. As for what we heard from Yemen, they put "أم" in place of the added alif and lām, saying "رأيت امْرَجُلَ" (I saw the man) and "قام امرجل" (the man stood), meaning "الرجل". It is not likely that ﴿أَمْ أَنَآ خَيْرٌ﴾ follows the dialect of the people of Yemen. Abū Zayd claimed that he heard an eloquent Bedouin reciting to them
[in the rajaz metre; this is the twelfth evidentiary verse]:
يا دَهرُ أَمْ كان مَشْيِي رَقَصا * بلْ قدْ تكونُ مشيتي تَرَقُّصا
(O Time, my walk was not a skipping gait — nay, my walk used to be a skipping.)
He asked him, and he said: "Its meaning is 'my walk was not a skipping'", so "أم" here is redundant (zāʾida). This is not known. ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbada said [in the ṭawīl metre; this is the thirteenth evidentiary verse]:
وما القلب أَمْ ما ذكرُهُ رَبَعِيَّةً * يُخَطُّ لَها من ثَرْمَداءَ قَلِيبُ
(What is the heart — or what is its remembering a woman of Rabīʿa, for whom a well is dug at Tharmadāʾ?)
He means "ما ذكرُهُ ربيعةً", making it a badal for "القلب". One of the jurists said: "Its meaning is that Pharaoh said ﴿أَفلاَ تُبْصِرُونَ﴾ or are you seeing?" The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; this is the fourteenth evidentiary verse]:
فَيا ظبيةَ الوعساءِ بين جُلاجِلٍ * وبينَ النَّقا أَأَنتِ أَمْ أُمُّ سالِمِ
(O gazelle of the sandy plain between Julājil and the dune — is it you or Umm Sālim?)
He means: "أَأَنت أَحسن أَمْ أمُّ سالِم" (are you lovelier, or Umm Sālim?), implying "أَحْسَن". He means [in the verse]: "أليسَ أَنا خيراً من هذا الذي هو مَهين" (am I not better than this one who is despicable?). It [أم] has another position in which it is cut off from the speech, as though you were turning back to its beginning. He said ﴿لاَ رَيْبَ مِن رَّبِّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ﴿أَمْ يَقُولُونَ ٱفْتَرَاهُ﴾; this had no question before it. This is the saying of the Arabs: "إنَّها لإِبل" (they are camels), and then they say * "أَمْ شاءٌ" (or rather sheep?), [and their saying]** "لقد كان كذا وكذا أَمْ حَدَّثتُ نفسي" (such-and-such happened — or did I talk to myself?) [Translator's note: the asterisks appear thus in the source], and like the poet's saying [in the kāmil metre; this is the fifteenth evidentiary verse]:
كَذَبَتْكَ عَينُكَ أَمْ رأيتَ بواسِطٍ * غَلَسَ الظَلامِ مِنَ الرَّبابِ خيالا
(Did your eye deceive you, or did you see at Wāsiṭ, in the last darkness of night, a phantom of al-Rabāb?)
His words ﴿أَمْ يَقُولُونَ ٱفْتَرَاهُ﴾ are not [said] because it is doubt; rather He said this to show the ugliness of what they did, as you say "ألستَ الفاعلَ كذا وكذا" (are you not the one who did such-and-such?), not asking but rebuking him. Then He said ﴿بَلْ هُوَ ٱلْحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ﴾. There is much like this in the Quran. He said ﴿فَذَكِّرْ فَمَآ أَنتَ بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ بِكَاهِنٍ وَلاَ مَجْنُونٍ﴾, then He said ﴿أَمْ يَقُولُونَ شَاعِرٌ نَّتَرَبَّصُ بِهِ﴾ [and] ** ﴿أَمْ عِندَهُمْ خَزَآئِنُ رَبِّكَ﴾; all of this is a resumptive question. "أَمْ" has no positions other than these two. [Here] He wanted to draw attention, then He mentioned what they said against him, meaning the Prophet ﷺ, to show the ugliness of what they said against him — as when you say to a man "ألْخَيْرُ أَحَبُّ إلَيكَ أَمْ الشَرّ" (is good dearer to you, or evil?), knowing he will say "good", but wanting to show him the ugliness of what he did. As for His words ﴿وَلاَ تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِماً أَوْ كَفُوراً﴾, He has forbidden him [to obey] the sinner and the disbeliever both. One of the jurists said: "'أوْ' can be like the wāw", and [the poet] said [in the mutaqārib metre; this is the sixteenth evidentiary verse]:
يُهِينُونَ من حقَروا شَأيَهُ * وإنْ كانَ فيهِمْ يَفِي أو يَبَرّ
(They humiliate one whose standing they despise, even if among them he keeps faith or acts righteously.)
He means "يَفِي وَيَبرّ" (keeps faith and acts righteously). Likewise it is [taken] by them here. But it is really like "كلُ اللحمَ أو التمرَ" (eat meat or dates) when you give him licence in things of this kind: if he ate all of it or one of them he would not disobey. So the prohibition falls on all of this in this sense, so that if he commits all or one of them, he [has] disobeyed, just as in the command, if he did one he obeyed. And He said ﴿وَأَرْسَلْنَاهُ إِلَىٰ مِئَةِ أَلْفٍ أَوْ يَزِيدُونَ﴾, its meaning being "ويزِيدُونَ" (and more). Its explanation in Arabic is that you say: "لا تجالسْ زيداً أو عمراً أَوْ خالِداً" (do not sit with Zayd or ʿAmr or Khālid): if he goes to one of them or all of them he is disobedient; just as when you say "إِجْلِس الى فلان أو فلان أوْ فلان" (sit with so-and-so or so-and-so or so-and-so) and he sits with one of them or all of them, he is obedient. This is its explanation in Arabic. I think those who said "'أو' is like the wāw" only said it because they saw it in its sense. As for ﴿وَأَرْسَلْنَاهُ إِلَىٰ مِئَةِ أَلْفٍ أَوْ يَزِيدُونَ﴾, He is only saying ﴿أَرْسَلْنَاهُ إِلَىٰ مِئَةِ أَلْفٍ﴾ "in people's estimation", then He said ﴿أَوْ يَزِيدُونَ﴾ "in people's estimation", because there can be no doubt on the part of Allah the Blessed and Exalted. Some people said: "'أو' here is like 'بل' (rather)". A man may say "لأَذْهَبَنَّ إلى كَذا وكَذا" (I shall certainly go to such-and-such), then afterwards something occurs to him and he says "أَوْ أَقْعُد" (or rather I will stay). So here He said ﴿أَرْسَلْنَاهُ إِلَىٰ مِئَةِ أَلْفٍ﴾ "in people's estimation", then He said ﴿أَوْ يَزيدون﴾ "in people's estimation", i.e. people do not doubt that they were more. The other view is like this: i.e. "such is the state of people concerning them", i.e. people are in doubt about them. Such too is the case of the cut-off "أم": if you wish you may take it in the sense of "بل", and that is a good approach. Mutammim ibn Nuwayra said [in the wāfir metre; this is the seventeenth evidentiary verse]:
فلو كانَ البكاءُ يردُّ شيئاً * بكَيْتُ على جُبَيْرٍ أو عِفاقٍ
على المَرْأَيْنِ إذْ هَلَكا جميعا * بشأنهما وحزنٍ واشتياق
(If weeping brought anything back, I would weep for Jubayr or ʿIfāq — for the two men, since both perished — over their affair, with grief and longing.)
And Ibn Aḥmar said [in the ṭawīl metre; this is the eighteenth evidentiary verse]:
فقلتُ البِثي شَهْرَيْنِ أَوْ نِصْفَ ثالثٍ * إلى ذاكَ ما قَد غَيَّبتَنِي غِيابِيا
(I said: stay two months, or half a third, until then — so long as my absence has kept me away.)
As for His words ﴿أَإِنَّا لَمَبْعُوثُونَ﴾ ﴿أَوَ آبَآؤُنَا ٱلأَوَّلُون ﴾, this wāw is a conjunctive wāw, as though they said ﴿أإِنا لَمَبْعُوثُون﴾ and it was said to them: "Yes, and your forefathers too", so they said ﴿أَوَ آبَآؤُنَا﴾. And His words ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَ ٱلإِنسَانُ﴾ ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَهْدِ لَهُمْ﴾ and the like are frequent in the Quran. The wāw is like the fāʾ in His words ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَهْدِ لَهُمْ﴾ and His words ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَدَّبَّرُواْ ٱلْقَوْلَ﴾. If you wish, you may make these fāʾs redundant (zāʾida); and if you wish, you may make them a response to something, as when they say "قد جاءني فلان" (so-and-so came to me) and he says "أَفَلَمْ أقض حاجته" (and did I not fulfil his need?), making this fāʾ connected to what precedes it.

akhfash:7-7.t: As for His words ﴿خَتَمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهمْ وَعَلَىٰ سَمْعِهِمْ وَعَلَىٰ أَبْصَارِهِمْ غِشَاوَةٌ﴾, the sealing does not fall on the eyes. He only said ﴿خَتَمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهمْ وَعَلَىٰ سَمْعِهِمْ﴾, then He said ﴿وَعَلَىٰ أَبْصَارِهِمْ غِشَاوَةٌ﴾ as a new, resumptive [sentence]. His words ﴿خَتَمَ ٱللَّهُ﴾: because that was due to their disobeying Allah, that wording was permissible, as you say "أَهَلَكتْهُ فُلانَةُ" (such-and-such a woman has ruined him) when he is infatuated with her, although she does nothing to him; for he perished in following her. Or "خَتَم" may mean that He judged them to be sealed.

akhfash:8-8.t:
Then He said ﴿وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يَقُولُ آمَنَّا بِٱللَّهِ وَبِٱلْيَوْمِ ٱلآخِرِ﴾,
making the wording singular, then He said ﴿وَمَا هُم بِمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾, making the wording plural. That is because ﴿مَنْ﴾ is singular in wording, yet it can be plural in meaning, and it can be dual. If you express its verb according to its meaning, that is correct; and if you make its verb singular according to its wording, that is correct. [And] among what has come of that is His words ﴿بَلَىٰ مَنْ أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُ للَّهِ وَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ فَلَهُ أَجْرُهُ عِندَ رَبِّهِ وَلاَ خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلاَ هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ﴾; and He said ﴿وَمِنْهُمْ مَّن يَسْتَمِعُونَ إِلَيْكَ﴾, and He said ﴿وَمِنهُمْ مَّن يَنظُرُ إِلَيْكَ﴾, and He said ﴿وَمَن يَقْنُتْ مِنكُنَّ للَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ وَتَعْمَلْ صَالِحاً نُؤْتِهَـآ أَجْرَهَا مَرَّتَيْنِ﴾: He said ﴿يَقْنُتْ﴾ according to the wording, because the wording of ﴿مَن﴾ is masculine, and made ﴿تَعْمَلْ﴾ and ﴿نُؤْتِهَآ﴾ according to the meaning. Some read ﴿ويَعْمَلْ﴾, according to the wording, because the wording of ﴿مَنْ﴾ is masculine. And some read ﴿وَمَنْ تَقْنُتْ﴾, according to the meaning, because it refers to a woman. This is a proof against whoever said: "The wording with مَن is not made according to the meaning unless ﴿مَنْ﴾ has the sense of ﴿الذي﴾ (who, relative); as for [in] conditional sentences and questions, the wording with ﴿مَنْ﴾ is not according to the meaning."
Their saying* this is an error, because this place in which ﴿وَمَنْ تَقْنُتْ﴾ occurs is conditional. [Translator's note: the asterisk appears thus in the source.] The Arabs have said "ما جاءَتْ حاجَتُكَ" (what has your need become?), making "جاءتْ" feminine although it belongs to "ما"; they made it feminine only because the meaning of "ما" is the need. And the Arabs, or some of them, said "من كانت أمّكَ" (who was your mother?), with the accusative. The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; this is the nineteenth evidentiary verse]:
تَعَشّ فإِنْ عاهدَتنِي لا تخونُني * نَكُنْ مثلَ مَنْ يا ذئبُ يَصطَحِبانِ
(Have your supper; if you pledge to me not to betray me, we shall be, O wolf, like two who keep company together.)
It is also related as ﴿تَعالَ فإن﴾ (come, and if…). [Here the dual verb is used with مَن.] And ﴿مَنْ﴾ has been treated like "رجل" (a man, indefinite). The poet said [in the ramal metre; this is the twentieth evidentiary verse]:
رُبَّ مَنْ انضجتُ غيظاً صَدْرَهُ * قد تَمَنَّى لِيَ شَرّاً لم يُطَعْ
(Many a one whose breast I made boil with rage has wished me harm, but was not obeyed.)
Were it not indefinite, like "رجل", "ربّ" would not fall on it.
Likewise (ما) is indefinite, except that it is like "شيء" (a thing). It is said that His words ﴿هَـٰذَا مَا لَدَيَّ عَتِيدٌ﴾ are of this kind: He made (ما) like "شيء" and did not make it like "الذي", so He said [in effect]: "ذا شَيْءٌ لَدَيَّ عَتيد" (this is a thing with me, ready). The poet said [in the khafīf metre; this is the twenty-first evidentiary verse]:
رُبَّ ما تَكْرَهُ النفوسُ من الأمْرِ * له فَرْجَةٌ كَحَل العِقالِ
(Many a thing in affairs that souls dislike has a release like the untying of a hobble.)
Were it not indefinite, like "مَنْ", "رُبَّ" would not fall on it. ﴿هذا مالَدَيَّ عَتِيدٌ﴾ may also be on another view: He gave a single predicate about both, as you say "هذا أحمرُ أخضرُ" (this is red-green). That is because some Arabs say "هذا عبدُ اللَّهِ مقبلٌ" (this is ʿAbd Allāh, coming). In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd: ﴿وهذا بَعلي شَيْخٌ﴾, as though he gave a single predicate about both; or it may be as though he made it nominative as an explanation: as though, when He said ﴿هذا ما لَدَيَّ﴾, it was said "What is it?", or He knew that this was wanted from Him, so He said ﴿عَتِيد﴾, i.e. what I have is ready. Likewise ﴿وهذا بَعْلِي شيخٌ﴾*. [Translator's note: the asterisk appears thus in the source.] The rajaz poet said [this is the twenty-second evidentiary verse]:
مَنْ يَكُ ذابَتٍّ فهذا بَتّى * مُقَيِّظٌ مُصَيِّف مُشَتِّى
(Whoever has a cloak — this is my cloak: for high summer, for summer, for winter.)
And He said ﴿إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ نِعِمَّا يَعِظُكُمْ بِهِ﴾: "ما" here is a noun that has no ṣila (relative clause), because if you made ﴿يَعِظُكُمْ بِهِ﴾ a ṣila of (ما), it would become like your saying "إنّ اللهَ نِعْمَ الشيء" (Allah, excellent is the thing) or "نعم شيئا" (excellent as a thing), and this is not [proper] speech. Rather you make (ما) a noun on its own, as you say "غَسَلتُه غَسْلاً نِعِمّا" (I washed it with an excellent washing), meaning by it "نِعْمَ غَسْلاً" (excellent as a washing). If it is said: "How can (ما) be a noun on its own when it is not spoken on its own?", I say: it is like "يا أيُّها الرجل" (O man), because "أي" here is a noun, and it is not spoken on its own until it is qualified; so (ما) has become like the qualified [noun] here. For when you say "غَسَلتُه غَسْلاً نِعِمّا", you only mean intensity and excellence, so this sufficed, so that it was spoken on its own. Similarly "ما أَحْسَنَ زيدا" (how handsome Zayd is!): (ما) here on its own is a noun. And his saying "اني مما ان اصنع كذا وكذا" (it is of my way to do such-and-such): (ما) here on its own is a noun, as though he said "إنّي مِن الأمر" or "منْ أَمْري صنيعي كذا وكذا" (it is of my affair that I do such-and-such). Among what has come according to the meaning is His words {كَمَثلِ الذي استوقدَ ناراً أَضاءَتْ ما حولَهُ ذهبَ الله بنورِهِم}, because "الذي" may be for the plural, as He said ﴿وَٱلَّذِي جَآءَ بِٱلصِّدْقِ وَصَدَّقَ بِهِ أُوْلَـٰئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْمُتَّقُونَ﴾. [Translator's note: the verse is quoted in the source with "فلما" omitted between "ناراً" and "أضاءت".]

akhfash:9-9.t:
As for His words ﴿يُخَادِعُونَ ٱللَّهَ وَٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾, although the mufāʿala form (reciprocal) only comes from two parties: He is only saying ﴿يُخَادِعُونَ ٱللَّهَ﴾ "in their own estimation, deluding themselves that they will not be punished, while they knew the opposite of that within themselves" — that is because of Allah's proof that falls upon His creation through knowledge of Him.
﴿وَمَا يَخْدَعُونَ إِلاَّ أَنْفُسَهُم﴾: some read ﴿يُخادِعُونَ﴾, saying "they deceive themselves by deceiving them", and this is how we read.
The mufāʿala form can come from one party in many things: you say "باعَدْتُه مُباعَدَةً" (I kept him at a distance) and "جاوزتُه مجاوزَةً" (I passed beyond him), in many things. He said ﴿وَهُوَ خَادِعُهُمْ﴾; this is by way of response: a man says to one who used to deceive him, when he gets the better of him, "أَنَا الذي خدعتُكَ" (I am the one who deceived you), though there was no deception from him, but he said that when the matter came to be in his hands. Likewise ﴿وَمَكَرُواْ وَمَكَرَ ٱللَّهُ﴾ and ﴿ٱللَّهُ يَسْتَهْزِىءُ بِهِمْ﴾ are by way of response. Scheming and mockery do not come from Allah; the meaning is that the scheming recoiled upon them and the mockery fell upon them.

akhfash:48-48.t:
Chapter on annexing [nouns of] time to the verb.
He said ﴿وَٱتَّقُواْ يَوْماً لاَّ تَجْزِي نَفْسٌ عَن نَّفْسٍ شَيْئاً﴾: He gave "the day" tanwīn because He made "فيه" ("in it") implied, and made it [the clause] an attribute (ṣifa) of "the day", as though He had said "a day in which no soul will avail another soul anything". Implying "فيه" is permissible only because annexing it [the noun of time] to the verb is permissible: you say "هذا يومُ يفعل زيد" ("this is the day Zayd does"). There is nothing among nouns that is annexed to a verb except nouns of time, and for that reason implying "فيه" is permissible. Some people said: "He only implied the hāʾ, meaning 'لا تَجْزِيهِ', and made this hāʾ a noun standing for the day as an object", just as you say "رأيتُ رجلاً يحبُّ زيدٌ" ("I saw a man Zayd loves"), meaning "يحبُّه زيد". In speech it is annexed: you say "اذكر يومَ لا ينفعُكَ شيء" ("remember the day when nothing will benefit you"), i.e. "the day of no benefit". That is because nouns of time may be annexed to the verb. He said ﴿هَـٰذَا يَوْمُ لاَ يَنطِقُونَ﴾, i.e. "the day of no speaking". It is also permissible in it [to say] "هذا يومٌ لا ينطِقون" [Translator's note: the text prints «يومُ» without tanwīn here; the argument requires the tanwīn form], if you imply "فيهِ" and make it an attribute of "يوم", because "يوم" is indefinite and you have made the verb belong to something connected with it and put the verb first. The verb is then entirely an attribute of the indefinite noun, as though you ran it on "the day" as an attribute of it, since it falls on something connected with it. Some of them have said ﴿هَـٰذَا يَوْمُ لاَ يَنطِقُونَ﴾ [Translator's note: presumably meant with tanwīn, «يومٌ», as a variant reading; printed as above], and likewise ﴿هَـٰذَا يَوْمُ ٱلْفَصْلِ﴾, and everything resembling this is like it. Nothing is annexed to the verb except time, except that they have said [in the wāfir metre; it is the sixty-eighth shāhid (evidentiary verse)]:
بآيةِ تقدِمون الخيلَ زُورا * كأنَّ على سنابِكِها مُداما
(By the sign that you lead the horses forward, swerving, as if there were wine on their hooves.)
[And they said] [in the wāfir metre; it is the sixty-ninth shāhid]:
أَلا من مُبْلِغٌ عَنّي تَميماً * بآيةِ ما تُحِبّونَ الطَّعاما
(Who will convey from me to Tamīm, by the sign that you love food?)
So he annexed "آية" to the verb. And they said: "إذهبْ بذي تَسْلَم" and "بذي تَسْلَمان" ("go, by your safety"), so his saying "ذي" is annexed to "تسلم", as though he had said "go, by [the one] of your safety". Nothing other than this is annexed to the verb. If you said in speech "واتقوا يومَ لا تَجزى نفسٌ فيهِ" without giving "the day" tanwīn, it would be permissible, as though you annexed while not intending to bring "فيهِ", and then it occurred to you afterwards, so you brought it; just as you say "اليومَ آتيكَ فيه" ("today I will come to you in it"), putting "اليوم" in the accusative because you brought "فيه" after you had made the accusative necessary. Some people said: "Implying 'فيه' is not permissible. Do you not see that you do not say 'هذا رجلٌ قصدتُ' ('this is a man I headed for') meaning 'إليه', nor 'رأيتُ رجلاً أرغَبُ' ('I saw a man I desire') meaning 'فيهِ'?" The difference between them is that in nouns of time there is what is not in others. And if you wish, you may treat it as an object by extension (fī al-saʿa), as though you said: "And fear a day which no soul will avail", then dropped the hāʾ, as you say "رأيتُ رجلاً أُحِبُّ" ("I saw a man I love") meaning "أحبه".
Chapter on feminine and masculine.
As for His saying ﴿تَجْزِي نَفْسٌ عَن نَّفْسٍ شَيْئاً﴾: it is like your saying "لا تَجْزِي عنك شاة" ("a sheep will not suffice for you"), "يجزى عنك درهم", "جَزى عنك درهمٌ" and "وجَزَتْ عنك شاةٌ". This is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, who do not use the hamza; and the Banū Tamīm say in this sense: "أَجْزَأَتْ عنهُ وتُجزِىءُ عنه شاة". And His saying "شيئا" is as though He said: "the sheep does not suffice with any sufficiency, and does not avail with any availing". And His saying ﴿عَن نَّفْسٍ﴾ means "مِنْها" ("from it"), i.e. it will not take its place.
As for His saying ﴿وَلاَ يُقْبَلُ مِنْهَا شَفَاعَةٌ﴾: He made [the verb of] the feminine noun masculine only because with every feminine [noun] that you separate from its verb it is good to make its verb masculine; except that this is ugly with humans and those like them that have reason, because the one that has reason is more deserving of the verb [agreement]. That is because these are made feminine and masculine only to distinguish between two meanings, while inanimate things like "the earth" and "the wall" have no meaning between them like that between man and woman. So everything that does not have reason is likened to inanimate things, and what has reason is likened to woman and man, as in His saying ﴿رَأَيْتُهُمْ لِي سَاجِدِينَ﴾: when they obeyed, they became like those that have reason. He said ﴿وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ﴾, making the verb masculine when He separated it from the noun, and He said ﴿لاَ يُؤْخَذُ مِنكُمْ فِدْيَةٌ﴾, and it is read ﴿تُؤْخَذُ﴾. That is also sometimes said of humans: they have claimed that they say "حَضَر القاضيَ امرأةٌ" ("a woman came before the judge"). As for the verb of the plural, it is made masculine and feminine, because the femininity of the plural is not the femininity of distinction. Do you not see that you make a group of males feminine, saying "هِيَ الرّجالُ" and "هِيَ القومُ"; and you name a man "بعال" and make it fully declinable, because this is a femininity like masculinity and is not [one of] distinction. But if you named him "عَناقِ" you would not make it fully declinable, because this is a femininity that does not belong to the male, and it is the distinction between masculine and feminine: you say "ذهب الرجل" and "ذهبت المرأة", distinguishing between them. And you say "ذهب النساء" and "ذهبت النساء", "ذهب الرجال" and "ذهبت الرجال". In the Book of Allah: ﴿كَذَّبَتْ قَوْمُ نُوحٍ ٱلْمُرْسَلِينَ﴾ and ﴿وَكَذَّبَ بِهِ قَوْمُكَ﴾. The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the seventieth shāhid]:
فما تركتْ قومي لقومِكَ حَيَّةً * تَقَلَّبُ في بَحْرٍ ولا بَلَدٍ قَفْرِ
(My people did not leave your people a living soul moving about at sea or in a barren land.)
And He said ﴿جَآءَهُمُ ٱلْبَيِّنَاتُ﴾ [and] ﴿وَقَالَ نِسْوَةٌ فِي ٱلْمَدِينَةِ﴾. [And] the poet said something stronger than this, having put the verb last; he said [in the mutaqārib metre; it is the thirty-second shāhid]:
[Translator's note: the number "thirty-second" is as written; it does not fit the surrounding sequence (sixty-ninth, seventieth, seventy-first).]
فإمَّا تَرَيْ لِمَّتِى بُدِّلَّتْ * فإنَّ الحوادِثَ أَوْداى بها
(If you see that my locks have been changed, it is the vicissitudes [of time] that have taken them away.)
He meant "أودتْ بها". Like the verb of a single woman, which may be made masculine, [so] he made this masculine. This masculine [agreement] is uglier with inanimate things and better with humans, and that is because every group of non-humans is feminine: you say "هي الحمير" ("they [fem.] are the donkeys"), and you do not say "هم". Except that they have said "أولئك الحمير", and that is because "أولئك" may be for feminine and masculine: you say "رأيت اولئك النساء" ("I saw those women"). The poet said [in the kāmil metre; it is the seventy-first shāhid]:
ذُمّى المنازِلُ بعدَ منزِلةِ اللِّوى * والعيشَ بعدَ أولئكِ الأيَّامِ
(Blame the dwellings after the dwelling at al-Liwā, and life after those days.)

akhfash:49-49.t:
As for His saying ﴿وَإِذْ نَجَّيْنَاكُم مِّنْ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ and ﴿وَإِذْ فَرَقْنَا بِكُمُ ٱلْبَحْرَ﴾ and many places [like them]: they depend only on what precedes them. He is only saying: "Remember My favour", "and remember when We saved you", "and remember when We parted the sea for you", "and remember when you said, O Moses, we will not endure". And some of them said "فرّقنا".
Chapter on أَهْل and آل.
And His saying ﴿مِّنْ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ يَسُومُونَكُمْ سُوۤءَ ٱلْعَذَابِ﴾, having said ﴿وَإِذْ نَجَّيْنَاكُم مِّنْ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾: He is only telling about what they used to meet from them. ﴿يَسُومُونَكُمْ﴾ is in the position of the nominative; and if you wish, you may make it in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), as though He said "and when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, [they] inflicting upon you"; and the nominative is on the basis of ibtidāʾ (beginning a new clause).
As for "آلُ", it is good when annexed to a particular noun, such as "أتيتُ آل زيد" ("I came to the family of Zayd") and "أهل زيد", "أهل مكةَ" and "آلَ مكةَ", "أهلَ المدينةِ" and "آلَ المدينةِ". If you said "أتيتُ آل الرجلِ" and "آل المرأةِ", it would not be good; but [one says] "أتيتَ آلَ اللّهِ", and they, as they claimed, are the people of Mecca. "آلُ" is not frequent with names of lands, though we have heard someone say that. It is only a hamza substituted in place of the hāʾ [i.e. آل from أهل], like "هَيْهاتَ" and "أَيْهَاتَ".

akhfash:50-50.t: ﴿وَإِذْ فَرَقْنَا بِكُمُ ٱلْبَحْرَ فَأَنجَيْنَاكُمْ﴾: He is saying, We parted between the two waters when you passed through it.

akhfash:51-51.t: He said ﴿وَإِذْ وَاعَدْنَا مُوسَىٰ أَرْبَعِينَ لَيْلَةً﴾, i.e. We appointed for him the completion of forty nights, i.e. the end of the forty, just as He said ﴿وَسْئَلِ ٱلْقَرْيَةَ﴾.
