This is like their saying "اليومَ أربعونَ يوماً منذُ خرجَ" ("today it is forty days since he left") and "اليومَ يومانِ" ("today it is two days"), i.e. "today is the completion of the forty" and "the completion of two days".

akhfash:55-55.t:
Chapter on the verb.
As for His saying ﴿حَتَّىٰ نَرَى ٱللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾, He is saying: "openly", i.e. "visibly, [with] what is between us and Him uncovered", just as you say "جَهِرَتْ الرَكِيَّةُ" ("the well was cleared") when its water had been covered by mud and that was removed until the water appeared [and] became clear.

akhfash:57-57.t:
As for His saying ﴿وَظَلَّلْنَا عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْغَمَامَ وَأَنزَلْنَا عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْمَنَّ وَٱلسَّلْوَىٰ﴾: "الغَمامُ" (clouds) — its singular is "غَمامةٌ", like "السَّحابِ", whose singular is "سَحابة". As for "السَّلْوَى", it is a bird for which no singular has been heard; it is likely that its singular is "سَلْوى", like its plural, just as they said "دِفْلَى" (oleander) for the singular and the plural, and "سُلامَى" for the singular and the plural; and they have also said "سُلامَيات". And they said "حُبَارَى" (bustard) for the singular, and for the plural they said "حُبارَيَات", and some of them said "حُبَارى" for the plural. The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the seventy-seventh shāhid (evidentiary verse)]:
وأَشلاءُ لَحْمٍ من حُبارَى يصيدُها * إذا نَحْنُ شِئْنا صاحبٌ مُتَأَلَّفُ
(And pieces of meat from bustards, hunted for us whenever we wish by a companion who is tamed [i.e. a trained falcon].)
And they said "شُكَاعَى" (a thorny plant) for the singular and the plural, and some of them said "شُكاعاة" for the singular.

akhfash:58-58.t:
His saying ﴿وَقُولُواْ حِطَّةٌ﴾, i.e. "say: 'Let there be from You a putting-down (ḥiṭṭa) of our sins'", just as you say to a man "سَمْعُكَ إلَيَّ" ("your hearing [be turned] to me"). It is as though it was said to them: "Say: 'O Lord, let there be from You a putting-down of our sins'". It has been read in the accusative on the basis that it is a substitute for pronouncing the verb; and everything that is a substitute for pronouncing the verb is accusative by that verb, as though He said "put down from us a putting-down", so it became a substitute for "حُطَّ". It resembles their saying "سَمْعٌ وطاعةٌ" ("hearing and obedience"): some of them say "سَمْعاً وطاعةَ" when they make it a substitute for "I hear a hearing and obey an obedience"; and when he uses the nominative, it is as though he said "my matter is hearing and obedience". The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the seventy-eighth shāhid (evidentiary verse)]:
اناخوا بأَيدي عُصْبَةٍ وسُيوفُهم * على أُمَّهاتِ الهامِ ضَرْباً شَآمِيا
(They made [their camels] kneel by the hands of a band, while their swords [were] on the crowns of the skulls, striking a Syrian stroke.)
And the other said [in the wāfir metre; it is the seventy-ninth shāhid]:
تَرَكْنا الخيلَ وَهْيَ عليهِ نَوْحاً * مُقَلَّدَةً أعِنَّتَها صُفُونا
(We left the horses mourning over him, with their reins hung on their necks, standing on three legs.)
Some of them said "وَهْيَ عَلَيْهِ نَوْحٌ", making them, by way of comparison, the mourning itself because of how much of it came from them, just as you say "إنَّما أنتَ شَرٌّ" ("you are nothing but evil") and "إنَّما هُوَ حِمارٌ" ("he is nothing but a donkey") by way of likeness; or you take the nominative as though he said "and they were over him possessors of mourning", and he dropped "possessors" and put "mourning" in its place. Like that is the saying of al-Khansāʾ [in the basīṭ metre; it is the eightieth shāhid]:
تَرْتَعُ ما رَتَعَتْ حتَّى إذا ذَكَرَتْ * فَإنَّما هِيَ إقْبالٌ وإدْبارُ
(She grazes as long as she grazes, until when she remembers, she is nothing but coming and going.)
Like it is ﴿قَالُواْ مَعْذِرَةً إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ [Translator's note: the passage explains the nominative reading «مَعْذِرَةٌ», though the verse is quoted in the accusative], as though they said "our admonishing them is an excuse"; and it was put in the accusative on [the basis of] "we excuse ourselves an excuse". And He said ﴿فَأَوْلَىٰ لَهُمْ﴾ ﴿طَاعَةٌ وَقَوْلٌ مَّعْرُوفٌ﴾, on [the basis of] His saying ﴿إِذَا جَآءَتْهُمْ ذِكْرَاهُمْ﴾ ﴿فَأَوْلَىٰ لَهُمْ﴾ ﴿طَاعَةٌ وَقَوْلٌ مَّعْرُوفٌ﴾: He made "obedience" a mubtadaʾ (subject) and said ﴿طَاعَةٌ وَقَوْلٌ مَّعْرُوفٌ﴾ is better than this; or He made "obedience" a mubtadaʾ and said "obedience and a fitting word are better than this". [Translator's note: the two alternatives are worded almost identically in the source; translated as written.] And Yūnus claimed that it was said to them "say حِطَةٌ", i.e. utter these words, as though it had been imposed on them to say this word in the nominative.

akhfash:59-59.t: He said ﴿فَأَنزَلْنَا عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ رِجْزاً مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ﴾, and He said ﴿وَٱلرُّجْزَ فَٱهْجُرْ﴾, and some of them said ﴿والرِجْزَ﴾. They mentioned that "الرُجْزَ" is an idol they used to worship; as for "الرِجْزَ", it is "الرِجْسُ" (filth) [and "الرِجْسُ" is "النَجَس" (impurity)]. And He said ﴿إِنَّمَا ٱلْمُشْرِكُونَ نَجَسٌ﴾, and "النَجَسُ" is dirt.

akhfash:60-60.t:
He said ﴿فَٱنفَجَرَتْ مِنْهُ ٱثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْناً﴾: the Banū Tamīm pronounce the shīn with a kasra, while the people of the Hijaz give it sukūn: ﴿ٱثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْناً﴾.
And His saying ﴿وَلاَ تَعْثَوْاْ فِي ٱلأَرْضِ مُفْسِدِينَ﴾ is from "عَثِيَ", "يَعْثَى"; and some of them said "يَعْثُو", from "عَثَوْتُ", so "أَنَا أَعْثُو", like "غَزَوْتُ", so "أنَا أَغْزُو".

akhfash:173-173.t:
He said: ﴿إِنَّمَا حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْمَيْتَةَ﴾. It is really "المَيِّتَةُ", lightened; likewise His saying ﴿بَلْدَةً مَيْتاً﴾ means "ميّتا", but they lighten the yāʾ, just as they say for "هيّن" (easy) and "ليّن" (soft): "هَيْن" and "لَيْن", lightened. The poet said [in the khafīf metre; it is the one hundred and thirty-third shāhid (attested verse)]:
لَيْسَ مَنْ ماتَ فاستراحَ بِمَيْتٍ * إنَّما المَيْتُ مَيِّتُ الأحْياءِ
(The one who has died and found rest is not [truly] dead; the dead one is only the dead among the living.)
So he used the doubled and the lightened form with one meaning. As for "الميتة" [with the vowel kasra on the mīm, i.e. al-mīta], it is [the manner of] death.

akhfash:175-175.t: He said: ﴿فَمَآ أَصْبَرَهُمْ عَلَى ٱلنَّارِ﴾. Some claimed that it is an expression of wonder (taʿajjub) at them, just as He said ﴿قُتِلَ ٱلإِنسَانُ مَآ أَكْفَرَهُ﴾, wondering at his disbelief. Others said ﴿فَمَآ أَصْبَرَهُمْ﴾ means: what made them endure, i.e. "what is it that made them endure?"

akhfash:176-176.t: He said: ﴿ذَلِكَ بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ نَزَّلَ ٱلْكِتَابَ بِٱلْحَقِّ﴾. The khabar (predicate) is implied, as though He were saying: "That is known to them because Allah sent down the Book", because He has informed us in the Book that that was said to them, so the Book is true.

akhfash:177-177.t:
He said: ﴿وَلَـٰكِنَّ ٱلْبِرَّ مَنْ آمَنَ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلْيَوْمِ ٱلآخِرِ وَٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةِ وَٱلْكِتَابِ وَٱلنَّبِيِّينَ﴾, then He said ﴿وَآتَى ٱلْمَالَ عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ﴾ … ﴿وَأَقَامَ ٱلصَّلاةَ وَآتَى ٱلزَّكَاةَ﴾. This is according to the beginning of the statement: "But righteousness is the righteousness of the one who believes in Allah, establishes the prayer and gives the zakat". Then He said ﴿وَٱلْمُوفُونَ بِعَهْدِهِمْ إِذَا عَاهَدُواْ وَٱلصَّابِرِينَ﴾: ﴿المُوفُونَ﴾ is nominative (marfūʿ) on [the meaning] "but [righteousness is] those who fulfil", meaning "the righteousness of those who fulfil"; since He did not mention "righteousness", He put ﴿الموفونَ﴾ in the place of righteousness, just as He said ﴿وَسْئَلِ ٱلْقَرْيَةَ﴾ and put it in the accusative by ﴿اسأل﴾ while meaning "the people of the town". Then He put ﴿ٱلصَّابِرِينَ﴾ in the accusative by an implied verb, just as He said ﴿لَّـٰكِنِ ٱلرَّاسِخُونَ فِي ٱلْعِلْمِ مِنْهُمْ وَٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ﴾, then said ﴿وَٱلْمُقِيمِينَ﴾ and put it in the accusative by an implied verb, then said ﴿وَٱلْمُؤْتُونَ ٱلزَّكَاةَ﴾, which is nominative either as a mubtadaʾ (subject) or by conjoining it to "الراسخين". The poet said [in the kāmil metre; it is the sixty-seventh shāhid]:
لا يَبْعُدَنْ قَوْمِي الذينَ هُمُ * سُمُّ العُداةِ وآفَةُ الجَزْرِ
النَازِلينَ بِكُلِّ مُعْتَرَكٍ * والطَّيِّبُونَ معاقدَ الأُزْر
(May my people never perish, who are poison to their enemies and the bane of the slaughter-camels; who alight in every battlefield, and whose waist-wrappers are knotted over chaste loins.)
Some say "النازلون" and "الطيبين"; some put both in the nominative and some put both in the accusative, as I have explained to you. And ﴿ٱلصَّابِرِينَ﴾ may be conjoined to ﴿ذَوِي ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ﴾: ﴿وَآتَى ٱلصَّابِرِينَ﴾ [i.e. "and gave … to the patient"].
And He said: ﴿فِي ٱلْبَأْسَآءِ وٱلضَّرَّاءِ﴾. He formed it on the pattern "فَعْلاء" and it has no "أَفْعَلُ" [masculine], because it is a noun, just as "أَفْعَل" occurs among nouns without a "فَعْلاء" alongside it, such as "أَحْمَدُ". They have also said "أَفْعَلُ" as an adjective without a "فَعْلاءُ" occurring for it: they said "أَنْتَ مِنْ ذاكَ أَوْجلُ" ("you are more afraid of that") and "أَوْجَرُ", but they did not say "وَجْلاءُ" or "وَجْراءُ"; both are from fear. And [from it is] "رجلٌ أَوْجَلُ" and "أَوْجَرُ" (a fearful man).

akhfash:178-178.t: He said: ﴿فَٱتِّبَاعٌ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ وَأَدَآءٌ إِلَيْهِ بِإِحْسَانٍ﴾, that is: "then upon him is a following-up in fairness or a payment to him with kindness", [incumbent] upon the one from whom it is claimed.

akhfash:180-180.t: He said: ﴿إِن تَرَكَ خَيْراً ٱلْوَصِيَّةُ لِلْوَالِدَيْنِ وَٱلأَقْرَبِينَ﴾: ﴿ٱلْوَصِيَّةُ﴾ is resumptive (on istiʾnāf), as though it were — and Allah knows best — ﴿إِن تَرَكَ خَيْراً﴾ then the bequest is ﴿لِلْوَالِدَيْنِ وَٱلأَقْرَبِينَ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ حَقّاً﴾.

akhfash:183-183.t: He said: ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾.

akhfash:184-184.t:
Then He said ﴿أَيَّاماً﴾, that is: fasting was prescribed [for] days. For you have occupied the verb with "fasting", so that it stands in the place of the fāʿil (agent), and "the days" became as though you had mentioned what was done in them.
And He said: ﴿فَمَن كَانَ مِنكُم مَّرِيضاً أَوْ عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍ فَعِدَّةٌ مِّنْ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾. He is saying "then upon him is a number": nominative. If you wish you may put "العِدَّةَ" in the accusative on [the meaning] "then let him fast a number", except that it has not been read [that way].
And He said: ﴿وَعَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ يُطِيقُونَهُ فِدْيَةٌ طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍ﴾. It has also been read ﴿فِدْيةُ طَعامِ مِسكين﴾, and this is not good: "food" is only an explanation of "the ransom", and the ransom is not put in a genitive construct with the food. His saying ﴿يُطِيقُونَهُ﴾ refers to the fasting. Some read ﴿يُطَوَّقُونَه﴾, that is: they undertake the fasting with hardship. Whoever reads ﴿مَساكِين﴾ means the whole month, because for each day there is a poor person; whoever reads ﴿مِسْكين﴾ is only stating what is due from him for missing one day.
And He said: ﴿وَأَن تَصُومُواْ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ﴾, because the light "أن" together with what it governs is equivalent to a noun, as though He had said: "and fasting is better for you".

akhfash:185-185.t:
﴿وَلِتُكْمِلُواْ ٱلْعِدَّةَ﴾: it is conjoined to what precedes it, as though He had said "and He wills that you complete the number" ﴿وَلِتُكَبِّرُواْ ٱللَّهَ﴾. As for His saying ﴿يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾, its meaning is only: He wills this in order to make clear to you. The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the one hundred and thirty-fourth shāhid]:
أُرِيدُ لأَنْسى ذِكْرَها فَكَأنما * تَمَثَّلُ لِي لَيْلى بِكُلِّ سَبيلِ
(I want to forget her memory, yet it is as though Laylā appears before me on every path.)
Its meaning is: I want this thing in order to forget her memory. Or he may have implied "أَنْ" after the lām and made the verb reach it by means of the preposition. He said ﴿فَهَدَى ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ لِمَا ٱخْتَلَفُواْ فِيهِ﴾, making the verb pass on by means of the preposition; the meaning is: He made them aware of the disagreement so that they abandoned it.
Then He said ﴿ شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ﴾ as an explanation of "the days", as though, when He said ﴿أَيَّاماً مَّعْدُودَاتٍ﴾, He explained them and said: "they are the month of Ramaḍān". Some put ﴿شَهْرَ رَمَضانَ﴾ in the accusative, [and that] is permissible as a command, as though He had said: "the month of Ramaḍān — so fast [it]"; or he made it an adverbial (ẓarf) on ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ﴾ … ﴿شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ﴾, that is: "in the month of Ramaḍān". And "رَمَضَان" is in the position of the genitive because "month" is put in a genitive construct with it, but it is a diptote.
And He said: ﴿ٱلَّذِيۤ أُنْزِلَ فِيهِ ٱلْقُرْآنُ هُدىً لِّلنَّاسِ وَبَيِّنَاتٍ مِّنَ ٱلْهُدَىٰ﴾. The position of ﴿هُدىً﴾ and ﴿بَيِّناتٌ﴾ is accusative, because He has occupied the verb with ﴿ٱلْقُرْآنُ﴾; it is like your saying "وجد عبد الله ظريفا" ("ʿAbd Allāh was found witty").
As for His saying ﴿وَٱلْفُرْقَانِ﴾, it is genitive on [the meaning] "and clear proofs of the Criterion".

akhfash:186-186.t: His saying ﴿يَرْشُدُونَ﴾: because it is from "رَشَدَ", "يَرْشُد"; and a dialect of the Arabs has "رَشِدَ", "يَرْشَد". It has also been read ﴿يُرْشَدُون﴾.

akhfash:188-188.t: He said: ﴿وَلاَ تَأْكُلُوۤاْ أَمْوَالَكُمْ بَيْنَكُمْ بِٱلْبَاطِلِ وَتُدْلُواْ بِهَا إِلَى ٱلْحُكَّامِ﴾: jussive by conjunction, and accusative if he makes it an answer with the wāw.

akhfash:189-189.t:
He said: ﴿هِيَ مَوَاقِيتُ لِلنَّاسِ وَٱلْحَجِّ﴾. He put ﴿الحَجّ﴾ in the genitive because He conjoined it to "الناس", so it became genitive by the lām.
And He said: ﴿وَلَـٰكِنَّ ٱلْبِرَّ مَنِ ٱتَّقَىٰ﴾, meaning "the righteousness of the one who is God-fearing".

akhfash:192-192.t: As for His saying ﴿فَإِنِ ٱنتَهَوْاْ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾, He means: then Allah is [forgiving and merciful] to them.

akhfash:193-193.t: His saying ﴿فَلاَ عُدْوَانَ إِلاَّ عَلَى ٱلظَّالِمِينَ﴾: because it is permissible for Him to say ﴿إِنِ ٱنتَهَوْاْ﴾ while knowing that they would not desist except some of them, so it is as though He had said: "If some of them desist, then there is no hostility except against the wrongdoers among them"; He left it implied. Just as He said ﴿فَمَن تَمَتَّعَ بِٱلْعُمْرَةِ إِلَى ٱلْحَجِّ فَمَا ٱسْتَيْسَرَ﴾, that is: then upon him is whatever is easy; and as you say "زيدا أكرمت" ("Zayd I honoured") meaning "I honoured him", and as you say "إلى مَنْ تَقْصُد أقصد" ("to whomever you head for, I head"), meaning "to him".

akhfash:194-194.t:
As for His saying ﴿فَٱعْتَدُواْ عَلَيْهِ﴾, Allah did not command aggression; He is only saying: "Bring upon them what used to be called aggression", that is: do to them as they did to you. Just as you say "إنْ تَعاطَيْتَ مني ظُلْما تعاطَيْتُهُ مِنْكَ" ("if you deal out wrong to me, I will deal it out to you"), and the second is not a wrongdoer. ʿAmr ibn Shaʾs said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the one hundred and thirty-sixth shāhid]:
جَزَيْنا ذَوِي العُدْوانِ بالأَمْسِ مِثْلَهُ * قَصاصاً سَواءً حَذْوَكَ النَّعْلَ بالنَّعْلِ
(Yesterday we repaid the aggressors with the like of it, an exact retaliation, as you cut one sandal to match the other.)

akhfash:195-195.t:
He said: ﴿وَلاَ تُلْقُواْ بِأَيْدِيكُمْ إِلَى ٱلتَّهْلُكَةِ﴾. He is saying: "into destruction" ("إلَى الهَلَكَةِ"). The bāʾ is redundant (zāʾida), like its being redundant in His saying ﴿تَنبُتُ بِٱلدُّهْنِ﴾, which is really "it produces oil". The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the one hundred and thirty-fifth shāhid]:
كَثِيراً بما يَتْرُكْنَ في كُلِّ حُفْرَةٍ * زفيرَ القواضِي نَحْبَها وَسُعالَهَا
(Often do they leave in every pit the groaning of [the beasts] that have met their end, with their gasping and coughing.)
He is saying "often do they leave", and he made the bāʾ and "ما" both redundant.

akhfash:196-196.t:
As for His saying ﴿فَإِنْ أُحْصِرْتُمْ﴾, it is because you say "أحصَرَني بَوْلي" ("my urine held me back") and "أحصرني مَرضِي" ("my illness held me back"), that is: it made me restrain myself. And you say "حَصَرْتُ الرجل", that is: I confined him, so he is "مَحْصور" (confined). Yūnus claimed from Abū ʿAmr that he would say "حَصَرْتُهُ" [when you block him] from every direction, and when you prevent him from going forward in particular, then you have "احْصَرْتُهُ"; and some of the Arabs say "أَحْصَرْتُهُ" for illness and the like of fatigue and exhaustion.
And He said: ﴿فَفِدْيَةٌ مِّن صِيَامٍ﴾, that is: then upon him is a ransom.
And He said: ﴿فَمَن لَّمْ يَجِدْ فَصِيَامُ ثَلاثَةِ أَيَّامٍ فِي ٱلْحَجِّ وَسَبْعَةٍ إِذَا رَجَعْتُمْ تِلْكَ عَشَرَةٌ كَامِلَةٌ﴾. He said ﴿عَشْرَةٌ كَامِلَةٌ﴾, having already mentioned seven and three, only to inform that they are sufficient, [and] not to inform of their number. Do you not see that His saying ﴿كَامِلَةٌ﴾ means only "complete (وافية)"?
They have mentioned that in the reading (ḥarf) of Ibn Masʿūd it is ﴿تِسْعٌ وَتِسْعُونَ نَعْجَةً﴾ "أُنْثى" (female). That is because speech is emphasised with what could be dispensed with, as He said ﴿فَسَجَدَ ٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةُ كُلُّهُمْ أَجْمَعُونَ﴾. One of the two may suffice, but repeating the expression makes it, as it were, more binding. Do you not see that you say "رأيت أَخَويكَ كِلَيْهِما" ("I saw your two brothers, both of them"), whereas if you said "رأيت أخويك" you would have had enough, and you bring "كليهما" as tawkīd (emphasis)? Some said concerning Ibn Masʿūd's "أُنْثى" that he only meant "مُؤَنَّثَةَ" (womanly, soft), describing her with that because that is something liked in women.
And He said: ﴿ذٰلِكَ لِمَن لَّمْ يَكُنْ أَهْلُهُ حَاضِرِي ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ﴾. When you pause you say "حاضري", because the yāʾ only dropped in continuous speech owing to the quiescence of the lām of "المسجد"; likewise ﴿غَيْرَ مُحِلِّي ٱلصَّيْدِ﴾. And His saying ﴿عَمَّ يَتَسَآءَلُونَ﴾ and ﴿فِيمَ أَنتَ مِن ذِكْرَاهَا﴾ and the like of these, which are not an inflectional letter (ḥarf iʿrāb) — the inflectional letter being the one on which the nominative, accusative and genitive fall — and such as "هو" and "هي": when you pause on it you have the choice; if you wish you add the hāʾ, and if you wish you do not. The Arabs have used the hāʾ in pause with the nūn of the plural and the nūn of the dual, saying "هُما رَجُلانِه" ("they are two men") and "مُسْلِمُونَهُ" ("Muslims"), and "قد قُمْتُهْ" when they mean "قَدْ قُمْتُ" ("I have stood up"); likewise whatever is not an inflectional letter, except that some of it is better than other, and it is more frequent with what has fatḥa. As for "مَرَرْتُ بأَحْمَرَ" and "يَعْمَرَ", the pause in these is not with hāʾ, because this can move away from this form [i.e. it can take other vowels]. Likewise whatever is not an inflectional letter but then changes from its state does not take the hāʾ when one pauses on it. As for His saying ﴿إِنِّيۤ أُرِيدُ أَن تَبُوءَ بِإِثْمِي وَإِثْمِكَ﴾, when you pause you say "تَبُوءْ", because it is "أَنْ تَفْعَلَ", and when you pause on "تَفْعَل" you do not vowel it. He said ﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَآ إِلَىٰ مُوسَىٰ وَأَخِيهِ أَن تَبَوَّءَا﴾ — [so] when you pause on it, because it is "أَنْ تَفَعَّلا" and you mean the action of two persons, this is how the pause on it is. He said ﴿وَلَقَدْ بَوَّأْنَا بَنِيۤ إِسْرَائِيلَ مُبَوَّأَ صِدْقٍ﴾: when you pause you say "مبوّأْ", and you do not say "مبوّءا", because it is muḍāf (the first term of a genitive construct), so when you pause on it there is no alif. Were you to keep the alif in it, you would say in pausing on ﴿غَيْرَ مُحِلِّي ٱلصَّيْدِ﴾: "محلين"; but it is like "رأيتُ غُلامي زيد" ("I saw Zayd's two servants"): when you pause you say "غلامي". And He said ﴿فَلَمَّا تَرَاءَى ٱلْجَمْعَانِ﴾: when you pause you say "تراءَى", and you do not say "تراءيا", because you have made "the two hosts" nominative by this verb; had you said "تراءيا" you would have brought a noun made nominative by this verb, namely the alif, and your saying "الجَمْعانِ" would not be [proper] speech except in another way.

akhfash:198-198.t:
He said: ﴿فَإِذَآ أَفَضْتُم مِّنْ عَرَفَاتٍ فَٱذْكُرُواْ ٱللَّهَ عِندَ ٱلْمَشْعَرِ ٱلْحَرَامِ﴾. He declined "عَرفاتٍ" fully (gave it tanwīn) because it is that plural which used to be declined; it was declined only because the kasra and the ḍamma on the tāʾ came to be equivalent to the yāʾ and the wāw in "مِسلمين" and "مُسلمون", since that is its masculine, and the tanwīn in the like of "عَرَفاتٍ" and "مُسْلِماتٍ" came to be equivalent to the nūn. So when [something] was named with it, it was left in its state, just as "مسلمون" is left in its state when [something] is named with it, by way of reproduction (ḥikāya). Some of the Arabs do not decline [this] when it is used as a name, and liken the tāʾ to the feminine hāʾ [in] the like of "حَمْدَةَ"; that is ugly and weak. The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the one hundred and thirty-seventh shāhid]:
تَنَوَّرْتُها من أَذْرِعاتٍ وأَهلُها * بيثربَ أَدْنى دارِهَا نظرٌ عالِ
(I glimpsed her fire from Adhriʿāt while her people were in Yathrib; the nearest of her abode is a lofty gaze away.)
Some do not give tanwīn to "اذْرِعات" or to "عانات", which is a place.

akhfash:203-203.t: He said: ﴿وَمَن تَأَخَّرَ فَلاۤ إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ لِمَنِ ٱتَّقَىٰ﴾. It is as though, when He mentioned this concession, He had informed of a matter, then said ﴿لِمَنِٱتَّقَىٰ﴾, that is: that is for the one who is God-fearing.

akhfash:204-204.t:
He said: ﴿وَيُشْهِدُ ٱللَّهَ علىٰ ما فِى قَلْبِهِ﴾, as he is the one who calls to witness. Some read ﴿وَيَشْهَدُ اللّهُ﴾, that is: Allah is the one who bears witness.
And He said: ﴿وَهُوَ أَلَدُّ ٱلْخِصَامِ﴾, from "لَدِدْتُ", "تَلَدُّ" (to be fiercely contentious), "هو أَلَدُّ" (he is most contentious), "هُمْ قَوْمٌ لُدٌّ" (they are a contentious people), "امْرَأَةٌ لَدّاءُ" (a contentious woman) and "نسوةٌ لُدُّ" (contentious women).

akhfash:207-207.t:
He said: ﴿وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يَشْرِي نَفْسَهُ ٱبْتِغَآءَ مَرْضَاتِ ٱللَّهِ﴾. He is saying "sells it", just as you say "شَرَيْتُ هذا المتاعَ", that is: I sold it; and "شَرَيْتُهُ" also means "I bought it". It is permissible in both meanings together, just as you say "إنَّ الجِلَّ لأَفْضَلُ المَتاعِ" ("al-jill is the best of the goods") and "إنَّ الجِلَّ لأَرْدَؤُهُ" ("al-jill is the worst of it"); on that basis it is permissible, with many like it. Likewise "الجَلَلُ" can be the great and can be the small; likewise "السَّدَفُ" can be darkness and light. The poet said
[in the ramal metre; it is the one hundred and thirty-eighth shāhid]:
وأَرى أَربْدَ قد فارَقَني * ومن الآرْزاءِ رُزْء ذُو جَلَل
(And I see that Arbad has left me; and among calamities there is a calamity of great weight.)
That is: great. Another said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the one hundred and thirty-ninth shāhid]:
ألا إنَّما أَبْكي لِيَوْمٍ لقِيتُه * بِجُرْثُمِ صادٍ كلُّ ما بَعْدَهُ جَلَلَ
(Indeed I weep only for a day I met at Jurthum Ṣād; everything after it is trivial.)
That is: small.
As for His saying ﴿ٱبْتِغَآءَ مَرْضَاتِ ٱللَّهِ﴾, it is accusative by the verb, namely "يَشْرِي", as though He had said "for seeking the pleasure of Allah"; when He removed the lām, the verb governed it. Like it is ﴿حَذَرَ ٱلْمَوْتِ﴾, and the like of this is plentiful. The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the one hundred and fortieth shāhid]:
واغْفِرُ عَوْراءَ الكرِيم ادّخارَه * وَأُعْرِضُ عَنْ شَتِم اللئيمِ تَكَرُّما
(I forgive the noble man's ugly word, to keep him in store, and I turn away from the base man's abuse out of nobility.)
When he omitted the lām, the verb governed it.

akhfash:10-10.t:
As for His words ﴿فَزَادَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ مَرَضاً﴾: whoever pronounces it full (tafkhīm) gives the zāy fatḥa and says ﴿زَادَهم﴾, and whoever inclines it (imāla) gives the zāy a kasra [quality] and says ﴿زادهم﴾, because it is from "زِدت" (I increased), whose first letter has kasra. Some Arabs incline what is of this kind — they are some of the people of the Hijaz — and they also say ﴿وَلِمَنْ خِافَ مَقَامَ رَبِّهِ﴾, ﴿فَٱنكِحُواْ مَا طِابَ لَكُمْ مِّنَ ٱلنِّسَآءِ﴾ [and] ﴿وَقَدْ خِابَ﴾. They do not say ﴿قِال﴾ or (زِار), because one says (قُلْتُ) and (زُرْتُ), whose first letter has ḍamma. They only do this with what has kasra on its first letter in the "فعلتُ" form, except that they tend towards the kasra just as they tend towards the yāʾ in His words ﴿وَسَقِاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ﴾ and ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّاهَا﴾. All of that is also read with tafkhīm. As for what is of this kind from roots with final wāw, where [the wāw] is the third [letter], as in ﴿وَٱلْقَمَرِ إِذَا تَلاَهَا﴾ and ﴿وَٱلأَرْضِ وَمَا طَحَاهَا﴾,
many Arabs pronounce it full and do not incline it, because it is not a yāʾ towards which one could incline, since it is from "طَحَوْتُ" and "تَلَوْتُ". When it is the fourth letter or beyond, they incline it, and imāla is the proper way, because it has then turned into a yāʾ. Do you not see that you say "غَزَوْتُ" and "أَغْزَيْتُ"? Similar is ﴿وَٱللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَاهَا﴾. And ﴿قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ﴾ and ﴿وَٱلنَّهَارِ إِذَا تَجَلَّىٰ﴾: he inclined them because [the final letter] is the fourth; "تَجَلّى" has its "فَعلْتُ" form with wāw, since it is from "جَلَوْت"; "زكا" is from "زَكَوْتُ يزكو"; and ﴿وَٱللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَاهَا﴾ is from "الغشاوة" (covering).
Many people do incline what has wāw, such as (تَلاِها) and (طَحِاها), because the wāw often turns into yāʾ, as in their saying (حِير) for (حُور), "مَشِيب" for "مَشُوب", and they said "أَرْضٌ مَسْنِيّة" (a watered land) when the rain waters it (يسنوها). So they inclined it towards the yāʾ, because it turns into it.
They inclined everything of the patterns "فَعْلى" and "فُعْلى", like "بُشْرى", "مَرْضى" and "سَكْرى", because if this were put in the dual it would be with yāʾ, so they inclined towards it.
As for His words ﴿بِمَا كَانُوا يَكْذِبُونَ﴾: (يُكَذِّبُونَ) [means] they deny, which is disbelief. Some read (يَكْذِّبُونَ) [Translator's note: so vocalised in the source, though described as the light form, i.e. يَكْذِبُونَ], light, and that is how we read, meaning "they lie against Allah and against the messengers". He made "ما" and the verb a noun standing for the maṣdar (verbal noun), just as "أنْ" and the verb were made a noun standing for the maṣdar in his saying "أُحبُّ أَنْ تأتِيني" (I would like you to come to me). As for the meaning, it is only "بكذِبهِم" (because of their lying) and "تَكْذيبِهِم" (their denying). He inserted "كان" to report that it was in the past, as you say "ما أحسنَ ما كانَ عبدُ الله" (how good ʿAbd Allāh was!): you are wondering at ʿAbd Allāh, not at his "being"; the wonder falls on his being only in the wording. And He said ﴿فَٱصْدَعْ بِمَا تُؤْمَرُ﴾; this is not in the sense of "فاصدع بالذي تؤمر به" (proclaim what you are commanded with); if it had this meaning it would not be [complete] speech until you brought "به". Rather [it is] "إصدع بالأمر" (proclaim the command): He made "ما تؤمر" a single noun. And He said ﴿ولاَ تَحْسَبَنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ بِمَآ أَتَوْاْ﴾, saying "بالإِتيان" (in the coming/doing), making "ما" and "أَتَوْا" a noun standing for the maṣdar. If you wish, you may say "أَتَوْا" here means "جاءُوا" (they brought), as though He says "بما جاءوا", meaning "جاءوه" (what they brought), as you say "يفرحون بما صنعوا" (they rejoice in what they did), i.e. "بما صنعوه". There is much like this in the Quran. Its implied form is "بكونِهم يكذبون" (because of their being [people who] lie), so "يكذبون" is the object of "كان", as you say "سرني زيد بِكونه يعقل" (Zayd pleased me by his being one who reasons), i.e. by his being rational.

akhfash:11-11.t:
As for His words ﴿وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ﴾: some give its first letter ḍamma, because it has the sense of "فُعِلَ" (passive), and he wants to leave its first letter with ḍamma to indicate its meaning. Some give it kasra, because a vowelless yāʾ does not come after a letter with ḍamma; kasra is the analogical form. Some say in speech "قد قُولَه له" (it has been said to him) and "قد بُوع المتاع" (the goods have been sold), when he means "قَدْ بِيع" and "قِيل": he made it a wāw when what precedes it had ḍamma, because a vowelless yāʾ does not come after a letter with ḍamma. Some give a trace of ḍamma (rawm) in "قُيل", like their giving a trace of kasra in "رِدَّ". It is a dialect of some Arabs to say "رِدَّ" (it was returned), giving the rāʾ kasra and putting on it the vowel of the dāl that is in the position of the ʿayn (second radical). Some do not give the rāʾ kasra but give it a hint (ishmām) of kasra, just as one gives a trace of ḍamma in "قيل". Al-Farazdaq said [in the ṭawīl metre; this is the twenty-third evidentiary verse]:
 وما حِلَّ من جهل حُبا حُلَمائِنا * ولا قائل المعروفِ فينا يُعَنَّفُ 
(The sitting-cloths of our forbearing men have never been loosened through folly, nor is one who speaks what is right rebuked among us.)
We heard it recited like this by one of the Arabs.

akhfash:13-13.t:
As for His words ﴿أَنُؤْمِنُ كَمَآ آمَنَ ٱلسُّفَهَآءُ أَلا إنهَّمْ هُمُ السُّفهآءُ﴾, some people read both [hamzas] with full hamza, and they read ﴿سَوَآءٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ﴾ [and] ﴿وَلاَ يَحِيقُ ٱلْمَكْرُ ٱلسَّيِّىءُ إِلاَّ بِأَهْلِهِ﴾, and they read (أإِذا) and ﴿أَإِنّا﴾: in all of this they pronounce two hamzas. None of this is the speech of the Arabs except as an anomaly. Rather, when two hamzas from different [words] come together with nothing between them, one of them is lightened in all the speech of the Arabs except in this rare, anomalous dialect. That is because when two hamzas come together in a single word they always replace the second: if what precedes it has fatḥa, they make it a vowelless alif, as in "آدم", "آخر" and "آمن"; if what precedes it has ḍamma, it is made a wāw, as in "أُوْزُزْ" (incite!), when you command him to incite; and if what precedes it has kasra, it is made a yāʾ, as in "إِيْتِ" (come!). Likewise, if the second is vowelled with any vowel and the first has ḍamma or kasra, the second follows the first, as in the form "أن أفعل" from "أَأَب": [so] you say "أُووب". And as in "جاءَ" in the nominative, accusative and genitive. [Translator's note: the source is elliptical here.] As for [the first] with fatḥa, the second does not follow it when it is vowelled, because if it followed it, it would be made a hamza like it. Rather it stays according to its own position: if it has kasra it is made a yāʾ, if it has ḍamma it is made a wāw, and if it has fatḥa it is also made a wāw, because the fatḥa resembles the alif. When you need to give it a vowel you make it a wāw, so long as it has no known origin in yāʾ; this fatḥa has no origin in yāʾ, so wāw was made predominant in it, as in "آدم" and "أوادم". Therefore, when two hamzas meet and are from two different words, one of them is lightened, and the heaviness of the two did not reach the point that they be treated like the two that come together in a single word; and because of the two in a single word one never parts from the other, whereas these two change from their state, and each one of them on its own becomes heavier than they are in two words, because in two words each one is on its own. [Translator's note: this sentence is confused in the source; translated as written.] So lightening the second is more analogical, just as they replaced the second when they came together in one word; but the first may also be lightened. Whoever lightens the second in His words ﴿كَمَآ آمَنَ ٱلسُّفَهَآءُ ألا﴾ says ﴿السفهاءُ ولا﴾, making the alif in (ألا) a wāw. Whoever lightens the first makes the alif [i.e. hamza] in (السفهاء) like a wāw and pronounces the alif of (ألاّ) with hamza. As for ﴿أَأَنْذَرْتَهُمْ﴾, the first is not lightened because it is the beginning of the speech; a hamza at the beginning of speech is not lightened, because the lightened [hamza] is weakened until it becomes like a vowelless letter, and one does not begin with it. Some Arabs said (آإذا), (آأنذرتهم) and "آأنا قلت لك كذا وكذا" (did I tell you such-and-such?), so that when the interrogative alif is joined to a hamza, he separates them with an alif so that two hamzas do not come together. All of this has been said, and all of this people have read. When the hamza is vowelless, then in the dialect of those who lighten it, if what precedes it has kasra it becomes a yāʾ, as in ﴿أنبِيهم بأسمايهم﴾ and (نَبِّينا)* [Translator's note: the asterisk appears thus in the source]; if it has ḍamma they make it a wāw, as in "جونَه"; and if what precedes it has fatḥa they make it an alif, as in "راس" (head) and "فاس" (axe). If a vowelled hamza comes after a vowelless letter, they give the vowelless letter the vowel of what follows it and drop the hamza; they say [for] "في الارض" (in the earth): (فِلَرْض), [and for] ﴿مَا لَكُمْ مِّنْ إِلَـٰهٍ﴾: (مِنِلاهٍ). They give the vowelless letter whatever vowel was on the hamza and drop the hamza.
When two hamzas from different words come together, the first* with kasra and the second with kasra, and you want to lighten the second, you make it between a vowelless yāʾ and a hamza (bayna bayna), because a vowelless yāʾ comes after a kasra, as in "هؤلاء يماء الله" (these are the bondswomen of Allah): you make the second "between-between" and pronounce the first in full. [Translator's note: the asterisk appears thus in the source.] If the second has fatḥa, as in "هؤلاء أخواتك" (these are your sisters), or ḍamma, as in "هؤلاء أُمَّهاتُك" (these are your mothers), you do not make it between-between but make it a pure yāʾ, because of the kasra before it; for you make the [hamza] with fatḥa between a vowelless alif and hamza, and the one with ḍamma between a vowelless wāw and hamza, when you want between-between, and this does not hold after a kasra. Whether the first is with hamza or without hamza is the same when you want to lighten the second. Of that is their saying "مِئين" and "مَئير" in the speech of those who lighten. If the letter has fatḥa and is followed by a hamza with fatḥa, kasra or ḍamma, it is made between-between, because after a fatḥa there can come a vowelless alif, a vowelless yāʾ, as in "البَيْع" (selling), and a vowelless wāw, as in "القَوْل" (saying). This is like ﴿يَتَفَيَّؤُا ظِلاَلُهُ﴾, ﴿وَيُمْسِكُ ٱلسَّمَآءَ أَن تَقَعَ عَلَى ٱلأَرْضِ﴾, ﴿آاذا﴾ and ﴿آانا﴾: when you lighten the second in all of these you make it between-between. What we choose is lightening the second when two hamzas come together, except that we pronounce both fully in teaching, intending thereby completeness. Lightening the second is the reading of the people of Medina, and pronouncing both fully is the reading of the people of Kufa and some of the people of Basra. Whoever claims that the hamza does not follow the kasra when it is lightened while vowelled, but is put according to its own position, is obliged to say "هذا قارِوٌ" (this is a reader), "هؤلاء قارِوُونَ" and (يستهزِوون). This is not the speech of those Arabs who lighten; they only say ﴿يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ and ﴿قارِئون﴾.
When what precedes the hamza has ḍamma and it [also has ḍamma], you make it between-between. [Translator's note: the source reads "وهي جعلتها", evidently with a word missing; supplied from context.] If it has kasra or fatḥa, it is not between-between when what precedes it has ḍamma, because the one with fatḥa is between a vowelless alif and hamza, and the one with kasra is between a vowelless yāʾ and hamza, and this does not occur after a ḍamma. Rather you make it a wāw after a ḍamma when it has kasra or fatḥa; you make it a pure wāw, because they follow what precedes them, as in "مررت بأكمُوٍ" (I passed by hillocks), "رأيت أكمُواً" (I saw hillocks) and "هذا غلامُوَبيكَ" (this is your father's servant): you make it a wāw when you want to lighten, unless the [hamza] with kasra is separated, in which case it stays according to its own position, because it has become distant.
Besides this, the wāw may be changed into yāʾ, as in "هذا غلاميخوانك" (this is your brothers' servant) and (وَلاَ يَحِيقُ ٱلْمَكْرُ ٱلسَّيِّىءُ يلا).
When they [the forms] have the sense of "فُعِلَ" (passive) and the hamza is in the position of the ʿayn, it is made between-between, because a vowelless yāʾ can come after a ḍamma: for "قُيْلَ" they say "قِيلَ". Similarly "سُيِل" (was asked) and "رُيِس" (was made chief): he makes it * between-between when lightening and leaves what precedes it with ḍamma. [Translator's note: the asterisk appears thus in the source.] As for "رُوِس", it is not "فُعِلَ" but "فُعْلَ", so it became a wāw because it comes after a ḍamma together with it in one word.

akhfash:14-14.t:
His words ﴿وَإِذَا لَقُواْ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ قَالُوۤا آمَنَّا﴾: He dropped the wāw [in pronunciation] because it was a vowelless letter that met the lām, which is vowelless, so it went because of its vowellessness, and there was no need to give it a vowel, since what remains is an indication of the plural. Likewise every wāw of this kind preceded by a ḍamma. When what precedes it has fatḥa, the wāw must be given a vowel, because if you dropped it the meaning could not be inferred, as in ﴿ٱشْتَرُواْ ٱلضَّلاَلَةَ﴾. The wāw was given ḍamma because if you said "اشتر الضلالة", dropping the wāw, it would not be known that it is plural. You gave it ḍamma only because the letter that went from the word had ḍamma, so it [the ḍamma] came to stand in its place. Some people read — and it is a dialect of some Arabs — ﴿ٱشْتَرَوِاْ ٱلضَّلاَلَةَ﴾: when they found a vowelless letter that had met a vowelless letter, they gave it kasra, as they do in other places; this is an anomalous dialect.
As for His words ﴿ وَإِذَا خَلَوْاْ إِلَىٰ شَيَاطِينِهِمْ﴾, you say "خلوت الى فلان في حاجة" (I was alone with so-and-so about a matter), as you say "خلوت بفلان", except that "خلوت بفلان" has two meanings: one is this, and the other is "I mocked him". "إلى" may stand in place of "مَعَ" (with), as in ﴿مَنْ أَنصَارِيۤ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ﴾, just as "من" has the sense of (علىَ) in His words ﴿وَنَصَرْنَاهُ مِنَ ٱلْقَوْمِ﴾*, i.e. against the people [Translator's note: the asterisk appears thus in the source]; and just as the bāʾ has the sense of "على" in his saying "مَرَرتُ بِهِ" and "مَرَرْتُ عليه" (I passed by him). In the Book of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿مَّنْ إِن تَأْمَنْهُ بِدِينَارٍ﴾, meaning "على دينار" (with a dinar). And just as "في" has the sense of "على", as in ﴿فِي جُذُوعِ ٱلنَّخْلِ﴾, meaning "على جُذوعِ النَخْل" (on the trunks of palm trees). Yūnus claimed that the Arabs say "نزلت في أبيك" (I stayed in your father), meaning "عليه" (with him), and they say "ظفِرتُ عليه", i.e. "بِهِ" (I got hold of him), and "رضيتُ عليه", i.e. "عَنْه" (I was pleased with him). The poet said [in the wāfir metre; this is the twenty-fourth evidentiary verse]:
 اذا رضِيتْ عَلَيَّ بنو قُشَيْر * لَعَمْرُ اللّهِ أعجبَنَي رِضاها
(When the Banū Qushayr are pleased with me — by the life of Allah, their pleasure delights me.)

akhfash:15-15.t: As for His words ﴿وَيَمُدُّهُمْ فِي طُغْيَانِهِمْ يَعْمَهُونَ﴾, it has the sense of "ويَمُدُّ لَهُم" (and He gives them rein), just as the Arabs said "الغلام يلعب الكِعاب" (the boy plays the knucklebones), meaning "يلعب ** بالكِعاب" (plays with the knucklebones) [Translator's note: the asterisks appear thus in the source]. That is because they say "قد مَدَدْتُ له" (I gave him rein), and "أَمْدَدْتُه" (I supplied him) in a different sense, which is His words, exalted be His praise, ﴿وَأَمْدَدْنَاهُم بِفَاكِهَةٍ﴾; and He said ﴿وَلَوْ جِئْنَا بِمِثْلِهِ مَدَداً﴾. Some read (مِدادا), and (مَدّا) [is] from "أَمْدَدْناهُم". You say "مَدّ النهرُ فهو مادّ" (the river swelled, so it is swelling) and "أَمَدّ الجُرُح فهو مُمِدّ" (the wound suppurated, so it is suppurating). Yūnus said: "What concerns evil is 'مدَدْت', and what concerns good is 'أَمْدَدْت'." [So] you speak as I have explained to him: when you mean that you left him [to go on], you say "مَدَدْتُ له", and when you mean that you gave him, you say "أَمْدَدْتُه".

akhfash:16-16.t:
His words ﴿فَمَا رَبِحَتْ تِّجَارَتُهُمْ﴾: this follows the Arabs' saying "خاب سعيُك" (your effort failed), when it is really he who failed; He only means "فما رَبحوا في تجارتهم" (they did not profit in their trade). Similar is ﴿بَلْ مَكْرُ ٱلْلَّيْلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ﴾ [and] ﴿وَلَـٰكِنَّ ٱلْبِرَّ مَنْ آمَنَ بِٱللَّهِ﴾, which is really "ولكنّ البرَّ برُّ من آمنَ بالله" (but righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in Allah). The poet said [in the mutaqārib metre; this is the twenty-fifth evidentiary verse]:
* وكيفَ تُواصِلُ من أصْبَحَتْ خَلاَلتُه كأبي مَرْحَبِ *
(How can you keep ties with one whose friendship has become like Abū Marḥab['s]?)
And the poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; this is the twenty-sixth evidentiary verse]:
وَشَرُّ المنايا مَيِّتٌ وَسْطَ أَهْلِهِ * كهُلْكِ الفتاةِ أسلَمَ الحَيّ حاضره
(The worst of deaths is one dying amid his family, like the perishing of a young woman whom the tribe's dwellers have abandoned.)
He only means "وشر المنايا منية ميّت وسط اهله" (the worst of deaths is the death of one dying amid his family). Similar is "اكثرُ شربي الماءُ" (most of my drinking is water) and "أكثر أكلي الخبرُ" [Translator's note: so in the source, for "الخبز", bread] (most of my eating is bread), although your eating is not bread nor your drinking water; rather you mean "most of my eating is the eating of bread, and most of my drinking is the drinking of water". He said ﴿وَسْئَلِ ٱلْقَرْيَةَ﴾, meaning "the people of the town", and (والعِيرَ), i.e. "and ask the people of the caravan". And He said ﴿وَمَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ كَمَثَلِ ٱلَّذِي يَنْعِقُ﴾; it is really — and Allah knows best — "مثَلُكُم ومثلُ الذين كَفَروا كمثلِ الناعِقِ والمنعوقِ بهِ" (the likeness of you and of those who disbelieve is as the likeness of the one who shouts and the one shouted at). This speech was omitted, and what remained indicated its meaning. There is much like this in the Quran. Some said ﴿وَمَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ كَمَثَلِ ٱلَّذِي يَنْعِقُ﴾ means "their likeness, in their calling upon the gods, is as the likeness of the one who shouts at sheep", because their gods neither hear nor understand, just as sheep neither hear nor understand.

akhfash:17-18.t:
His words ﴿كَمَثَلِ ٱلَّذِي ٱسْتَوْقَدَ نَاراً﴾: it has the sense of "أَوْقَد" (kindled), like his saying "فلم يستجبه", i.e. "فلم يُجِبْهُ" (he did not answer him). The poet said
[in the ṭawīl metre; this is the twenty-seventh evidentiary verse]:
وداعٍ دعا يا من يُجيبُ الى النَدى * فلم يَستَجِبْهُ عندَ ذاك مُجيبُ
(Many a caller called: "O who will answer [the call] to generosity?" — and no answerer answered him then.)
i.e. "فلم يُجِبْهُ".
And He said ﴿وَتَرَكَهُمْ فِي ظُلُمَاتٍ لاَّ يُبْصِرُونَ﴾, making (الذي) plural, so He said (وتَرَكَهم)* [Translator's note: the asterisk appears thus in the source], because "الذي" has the sense of a plural, just as "الانسان" (man) can have the sense of "الناس" (people).
And He said ﴿وَتَرَكَهُمْ فِي ظُلُمَاتٍ لاَّ يُبْصِرُونَ صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ فَهُمْ لاَ يَرْجِعُونَ﴾: it is nominative on the basis of "هُمْ صمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ" (they are deaf, dumb, blind), nominative as the khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject) [lit. "nominative by inception"]; had it been [made to follow] the first part of the speech, the accusative in it would have been good.
As for ﴿حَوْلَهُ﴾, it is accusative as a ẓarf (adverb of place/time; mafʿūl fīhi), because the ẓarf is accusative. The ẓarf is that in which a thing is, as the poet said [in the kāmil metre; this is the twenty-eighth evidentiary verse]:
هذا النهارُ بدا لَها من هَمِّها‌‌ * ما بالُها بالليلِ زالَ زوالَها
(This is by day what appeared to her of her care; what is the matter with her by night — may [the night] pass away as she passes!)
He made "النهار" accusative as a ẓarf; and if he wished he could make it nominative, with an implied [pronoun] in it. As for "زوالَها", it is as though he said: "أزالَ اللَّهُ الليلَ زوالَها" (may Allah make the night pass as she passes).

akhfash:20-20.t:
As for ﴿يَكَادُ ٱلْبَرْقُ يَخْطَفُ أَبْصَارَهُمْ﴾, some read (يَخْطِفُ) from "خَطَفَ"; this is rare and poor, hardly known. Yūnus related it as (يَخِطِّفُ), with kasra on the khāʾ because of the meeting of two vowelless letters. Some read (يَخْطَفُ), from "خَطِفَ يخطَفُ", and this is the good one; they are two dialect forms. Some said (يَخِطِّفُ) — this is the view of Yūnus — from "يَخْتَطِفُ", assimilating the tāʾ into the ṭāʾ because its point of articulation is close to that of the ṭāʾ. Some said (يَخَطِّفُ), transferring the fatḥa to the letter before it; and whoever gave kasra did so because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, saying ﴿يَخِطِّفُ﴾. Some said ﴿يِخِطِّفُ﴾, giving the khāʾ kasra because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, then giving the yāʾ kasra, making the [first] kasra follow the [second] kasra, which is before it [Translator's note: so in the source; logically the kasra of the khāʾ comes after the yāʾ], as they often make it follow in the speech of the Arabs: in this category they make kasra follow kasra, saying "قِتِلوا" and "فِتِحوا", meaning ["اقتِلوا" and]* "اِفْتحَوا". [Translator's note: the asterisk appears thus in the source.] Abū al-Najm said [in the rajaz metre; this is the twenty-ninth evidentiary verse]:
* تَدافُعَ الشِيبِ ولم تِقِتِّل *
(…like the jostling of grey-haired men who are not fighting one another.)
We heard it from the Arabs with kasra throughout. This is like "يِخِطِف" when its yāʾ is given kasra [because of the kasra of its khāʾ], which comes after it: he made** the latter follow the former. [Translator's note: the double asterisk appears thus in the source.]
His words ﴿وَلَوْ شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَذَهَبَ بِسَمْعِهِمْ﴾: some assimilate, making the first bāʾ vowelless, because they are two identical letters; and some give it a vowel, saying ﴿لَذَهَبْ بِسَمْعِهِمْ﴾. [Translator's note: the example as printed shows the vowelless (assimilating) form, though it is attached to those who give it a vowel; translated as written.] He made "السَمْع" (hearing) singular in wording although it is plural, because "السَمْع" can be plural and [can] be singular; [similar to it] is His words ﴿ خَتَمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهمْ وَعَلَىٰ سَمْعِهِمْ﴾; similar to it are His words ﴿لاَ يَرْتَدُّ إِلَيْهِمْ طَرْفُهُمْ﴾ and His words ﴿فَإِن طِبْنَ لَكُمْ عَن شَيْءٍ مِّنْهُ نَفْساً﴾; and similar to it is ﴿وَيُوَلُّونَ ٱلدُّبُرَ ﴾.

akhfash:61-61.t:
Chapter on the addition of "مِنْ".
As for His saying ﴿يُخْرِجْ لَنَا مِمَّا تُنْبِتُ ٱلأَرْضُ مِن بَقْلِهَا وَقِثَّآئِهَا﴾: (مِنْ) entered into it in the way you say in speech: "أهلْ البَصْرة يأكلون من البُرِّ والشَعير" ("the people of Basra eat [some] of wheat and barley"), and you say "ذهبتُ فَأصَبْتُ من الطَّعام" ("I went and obtained [some] of the food"), meaning "something", without mentioning the "something". Likewise ﴿يُخْرِجْ لَنَا مِمَّا تُنْبِتُ ٱلأَرْضُ﴾ [means] something, and He did not mention the "something". And if you wish, you may take it on the basis of your saying "ما رأيت مِنْ أَحَدٍ" meaning "ما رأيتُ أحَداً" ("I did not see anyone"), and "هلْ جاءك مِنْ رَجْلٍ" meaning "has a man come to you?". If you say, "This only happens in negation and interrogation", [the answer is that] it has come in other than that: He said ﴿وَيُكَفِّرُ عَنكُم مِّن سَيِّئَاتِكُمْ﴾, and this is neither interrogation nor negation. And you say "زيدْ مِنْ أَفْضَلِها" meaning "he is the best of them". And the Arabs say "قد كانَ مِنْ حَدِيثٍ فَخَلِّ عَنّي حتّى أذهب" ("there has been [some] talk, so let me go"), meaning "there has been talk". Comparable to it is their saying "هَلْ لَكَ في كذا وكَذا" ("have you [an interest] in such-and-such?") without saying "حاجَةُ" ("need"), and "لا عَلَيْكَ", meaning "لا بَأَسَ عَلَيْكَ" ("no harm on you").
As for His saying ﴿ٱهْبِطُواْ مِصْراً﴾, and He said ﴿ٱدْخُلُواْ مِصْرَ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ﴾: some people have claimed that in both of them He means "Miṣr" (Egypt) itself; but with a feminine noun of this kind, [like] "هِنْد" and "جُمْل", some of the Arabs make it fully declinable and some do not. Some of them said: "As for the one in [Sūrat] Yūsuf, He means Egypt itself by it, and the one in [Sūrat] al-Baqara, He means by it a city among the cities."
As for His saying ﴿وَبَآءُو بِغَضَبٍ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ﴾, He is saying: "they returned with it", i.e. it came to be upon them. You say "باء بِذَنْبِهِ يَبُوءُ بَوْءاً" ("he returned bearing his sin"). And He said ﴿إِنِّيۤ أُرِيدُ أَن تَبُوءَ بِإِثْمِي وَإِثْمِكَ﴾, which is like it.
Chapter on the explanation of the hamza.
As for His saying ﴿وَيَقْتُلُونَ ٱلنَّبِيِّينَ بِغَيْرِ ٱلْحَقِّ﴾ [and] ﴿وَيَقْتُلُونَ ٱلأَنْبِيَآءَ﴾: the whole body of the Arabs says all of that.
Among them are those who say ﴿النُّبَاءَ﴾: those are the ones who pronounce "النَبِىء" with a hamza, and they treat it like "عَريف" and "عُرَفاء". Those who do not use the hamza in it treat it like the yāʾ-final words, so it becomes like "وَصِيّ" and "أَوْصِياء"; and they also say "هُمْ وَصِيُّونَ". That is because the Arabs convert a word from the hamza until it becomes like the yāʾ-final words. They agree on dropping the hamza in [words] such as "المِنْسأَةِ" (staff), and hardly anyone pronounces it with a hamza except in the Quran, for most of them read it with the hamza, and that is how we read it; it is from "نَسَأْتُ". And what comes from "رَأَيْتُ" in the pattern "يَفْعَلُ", "تَفْعَلُ", "نَفْعَلُ" or "أَفْعَلُ" comes without the hamza, and that is because the letter that was before the hamza is quiescent, so the hamza was dropped and the letter before it was given its vowel, just as you say "مَنَ ابوك" ("who is your father?"). He said ﴿أَفَتُمَارُونَهُ عَلَىٰ مَا يَرَىٰ﴾, and He said ﴿لَتَرَوُنَّ ٱلْجَحِيمَ﴾, and He said ﴿إِنَّيۤ أَرَىٰ مَا لاَ تَرَوْنَ﴾, and He said ﴿إِنَّا لَنَرَاكَ فِي ضَلاَلٍ مُّبِينٍ﴾. As for His saying ﴿أَرَأَيْتَ ٱلَّذِي يُكَذِّبُ بِٱلدِّينِ﴾ and ﴿أَرَأَيْتَ إِن كَانَ عَلَىٰ ٱلْهُدَىٰ﴾, and whatever of "أَرَأَيْتَ" is in this sense, there are two dialects in it: some of them use the hamza and some of them say "أَريْتَ". This is done only in this "أَرَأَيْتَ" that has been set for interrogation, because of its frequency. As for "أَرأَيْتَ زَيْداً" when you mean "have you seen Zayd [with your eyes]", it is only spoken with the hamza or with a lightened hamza; "أَرَيْتَ" is hardly said [here], because the other one became frequent in speech and so it was shortened, just as it was shortened in "[أَمَانَّه] ظريف", meaning "أَما إِنَّه ظَريفٌ" ("he is indeed charming"); [so] they shorten. And they also say "لَهِنَّكَ لَظَريفٌ", meaning "[لـ]إنَّكَ لَظَريفٌ" ("you are indeed charming"). But the hamza was dropped just as they dropped [something] in their saying [in the basīṭ metre; it is the eighty-first shāhid (evidentiary verse)]:
لاهِ ابنُ عَمِّكَ لا أَفْضَلْتَ في حَسَبٍ * عَنّي وَلا أَنَتَ دَيّاني فَتَخْزُوني
(By God, [you] your cousin — you do not surpass me in lineage, nor are you my master that you should govern me.)
And the poet said [in the kāmil metre; it is the eighty-second shāhid]:
أَرأيْتَ إنْ أَهْلَكْتُ مالِيَ كُلَّهُ * وَتَرَكْتُ مَا لَكَ فيمَ أَنْتَ تَلُومُ
(Tell me: if I have destroyed all my wealth and left yours alone, for what do you blame [me]?)
[So he used the hamza.] And the other said [in the mutaqārib metre; it is the eighty-third shāhid]:
ارَيْتَ امْرَءاً كنتُ لَمْ أَبْلُهُ * أَتَانِيْ وَقالَ اتَّخِذْنِي خَلِيلا
(Tell me of a man I had not tested, who came to me and said: "Take me as a close friend".)
So he did not use the hamza. And he said [in the kāmil metre; it is the eighty-fourth shāhid]:
يا خاتمَ النُّبَاءِ إِنَّكَ مُرْسَلٌ * بِالحَقِّ كُلُّ هُدَى السَّبيلِ هُداكا
(O Seal of the Prophets, you are sent with the truth; all guidance of the way is your guidance.)
As for His saying ﴿بِمَا عَصَوْا﴾, [then] He made it a noun here, like "disobedience", meaning "by their disobedience"; so He made "ما" and "عَصَوْا" a noun [i.e. an interpreted maṣdar (verbal noun)].

akhfash:63-63.t: His saying ﴿وَإِذْ أَخَذْنَا مِيثَاقَكُمْ وَرَفَعْنَا فَوْقَكُمُ ٱلطُّورَ خُذُواْ مَآ آتَيْنَاكُم بِقُوَّةٍ﴾: this depends on the earlier speech. He is saying: "Remember when We took your covenant and raised the Mount above you: take", He is saying: "and We said to you: 'Take'". Just as you say "أَوْحَيتُ إليْهِ: قُمْ" ("I revealed to him: stand"), as though one were saying "I revealed to him and said to him: 'Stand'"; and in your saying "I revealed to him" there was an indication that you had said [it] to him.

akhfash:65-65.t:
As for His saying ﴿وَلَقَدْ عَلِمْتُمُ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱعْتَدَواْ مِنْكُمْ فِي ٱلسَّبْتِ﴾, He is saying "and you have certainly known [i.e. been acquainted with]", just as you say "لقد علِمت زَيْداً وَلَمْ أَكُنْ أَعلَمُه" ("I have come to know Zayd, and I did not know him [before]"). And He said ﴿وَآخَرِينَ مِن دُونِهِمْ لاَ تَعْلَمُونَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ يَعْلَمُهُمْ﴾, saying "He knows them [is acquainted with them]". And He said ﴿لاَ تَعْلَمُهُمْ نَحْنُ نَعْلَمُهُمْ﴾, i.e. you are not acquainted with them; We are acquainted with them. And when you intend the other [kind of] knowing, you say "قَدْ عَلِمْتُ زَيْداً ظريفاً" ("I knew Zayd to be charming"), because you are speaking about his charm; if you said "قدْ عَلِمْتُ زَيْداً" [in that sense], it would not be [complete] speech.
As for His saying ﴿كُونُواْ قِرَدَةً خَاسِئِينَ﴾, it is because you say "خَسَأْتُهُ" ("I drove him away"), "فَخَسِىءَ", "يَخْسَأُ خَسْأً شديدا", so "هُوَ خَاسِىءٌ" and "هُمْ خاسِئُون".

akhfash:66-66.t: As for His saying ﴿فَجَعَلْنَاهَا نَكَالاً﴾: it [the pronoun] may refer to the apes, and it may refer to the punishment that befell them; that is why it was made feminine.

akhfash:67-67.t: As for His saying ﴿أَتَتَّخِذُنَا هُزُواً﴾: among the Arabs and the readers there are those who make it heavy [i.e. pronounce the zāy with a ḍamma], and among them those who make it light [with sukūn]. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar claimed that with every noun of three letters whose first letter has a ḍamma, some of the Arabs make it heavy and some make it light, such as "اليُسُر" [and "اليُسْر"], "العُسُر" [and "العُسْر"], and "الرُحُم" [and "الرُحْم"]. And some of them said ﴿عُذْراً﴾ light and ﴿أونُذُراً﴾ heavy, and this is frequent, and that is how we read. And this dialect that ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar mentioned also moves the second [letter] with a ḍamma.

akhfash:68-68.t: As for His saying ﴿إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةٌ لاَّ فَارِضٌ وَلاَ بِكْرٌ عَوَانٌ﴾: it is nominative (marfūʿ) and did not become accusative as the negated [noun] becomes accusative, because this is in meaning an attribute of the cow. The accusative negated [noun, after the lā of generic negation] is never one of its attributes; it is only a noun that is a mubtadaʾ (subject) with its khabar (predicate) implied. This is like your saying "عبدُ اللّهُ لا قائمٌ ولا قاعدٌ" ("ʿAbd Allāh is neither standing nor sitting"): you brought in "لا" for the meaning and left the inflection as it would be if there were no "لا" in it.

akhfash:69-69.t:
As for His saying ﴿بَقَرَةٌ صَفْرَآءُ فَاقِـعٌ﴾: "الفاقِعُ" is intensely yellow. And it is said "أَبْيضُ يَقَقٌ", i.e. intensely white, and "لِهاقٌ", "لَهَقٌ" and "لَهاقٌ"; and "أَخَضَرُ ناضِرٌ" (bright green), "أَحْمَرُ قانِىءٌ" (deep red), "ناصِعٌ" and "فاقِمٌ". And it is said "قَدْ قَنَأَتْ لِحْيَتُهُ" ("his beard has turned red"), so it "تَقْنَأُ قُنُوءا", i.e. it became red. The poet said [in the kāmil metre; it is the eighty-fifth shāhid (evidentiary verse)]:
............. * كَما قَنَأَتْ أَنامِلُ صاحِبِ الكَرْمِ
(… as the fingertips of the vineyard owner have turned red.)
And [it is also recited] "قاطِفُ الكَرْمِ" ("the grape-picker"). And another said [in the kāmil metre; it is the eighty-sixth shāhid]:
مِنْ خَمِرّ ذي نَطَفٍ أَغَنَّ كَأنَّما * قَنَأَتْ أَنامِلُهُ مِن الفِرْصادِ
([Wine poured] by a wine-seller with earrings, nasal of voice, as though his fingertips were reddened by mulberries.)

akhfash:70-70.t:
As for His saying ﴿إِنَّ ٱلبَقَرَ تَشَابَهَ عَلَيْنَا﴾: [then] He made "البَقَر" (cattle) masculine, like "التَمْر" (dates) and "البُسْر" (unripe dates), just as you say "إنَّ زيداً تَكَلَم يا فَتَى" ("Zayd has spoken, young man"). And if you wish, you may say (يَشّابهُ), which is the reading of Mujāhid: he made "البقر" masculine, meaning ﴿يَتَشابَهُ﴾, then assimilated the tāʾ into the shīn. Whoever made "البقَر" feminine said ﴿تَشّابَهُ﴾, assimilating; or, if he wished, he dropped the second tāʾ and put it in the nominative [i.e. the imperfect, تَشَابَهُ], as you say "إنَّ هذِهِ تَكَلَّمُ يا فَتِى" ("this [woman] is speaking, young man"). For in "تَتَشابَهُ" one of the two [tāʾs] is the tāʾ of "تَفْعَلُ" and the other is the one in "تَشابَهَتْ". So in the feminine its meaning is "تَفْعَلُ" [the imperfect], and in the masculine its meaning is "فَعَلَ" [the past], and "فَعَلَ" always ends in a fatḥa, as I mentioned to you; and the tāʾ is dropped when you intend the feminine, because you mean "تَشابَهَتْ", so it is "تَتشابهُ". Likewise everything [that is] of the kind of "البَقَرِ", where there is no difference between singular and plural [in it] except the hāʾ [tāʾ marbūṭa]: some of the Arabs make it masculine and some make it feminine, and some of them say "هي البُرُّ والشعير" ("it [fem.] is the wheat and the barley"). And He said ﴿وَٱلنَّخْلَ بَاسِقَاتٍ لَّهَا طَلْعٌ نَّضِيدٌ﴾, making it feminine according to that dialect, and He said "باسقات" in the plural because the meaning is a group. And Allah, exalted be His praise, said ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُزْجِي سَحَاباً ثُمَّ يُؤَلِّفُ بَيْنَهُ﴾, making it masculine in the dialect of those who make it masculine, and He said ﴿وَيُنْشِىءُ ٱلسَّحَابَ ٱلثِّقَالَ﴾, using the plural according to the meaning, because the meaning is that of [several] clouds. And He said ﴿وَمِنْهُمْ مَّن يَنْظُرُ إِلَيْكَ﴾ and He said ﴿وَمِنْهُمْ مَّن يَسْتَمِعُونَ إِلَيْكَ﴾, according to the meaning and the wording [respectively].
[Translator's note: «يَنْظُرُ» follows the wording and «يَسْتَمِعُونَ» the meaning; the source lists "the meaning and the wording" in that order.]
Some of them said ﴿إنَّ الباقِرُ﴾ [Translator's note: printed thus; presumably «إنَّ الباقِرَ»], like "الجامِل", meaning "cattle" and "camels". The poet said [in the kāmil metre; it is the eighty-seventh shāhid (evidentiary verse)]:
‌مالِي رأيتُكَ بعد أَهْلِكَ مُوحِشا * خَلِقاً كَحَوْضِ الباقِرِ المُتَهَدِّمِ
(Why do I see you, after your people [left], desolate and worn, like the crumbling trough of the cattle?)
And he said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the eighty-eighth shāhid]:
[فَإِنْ تَكُ ذا شاءٍ كَثِيرٍ فإنَّهُمْ] * ذَوُو جامِلٍ لا يَهْدَأُ اللَّيْلَ سامِرُهُ
([If you are the owner of many sheep, then they] are owners of camel herds whose night-talker does not rest all night.)
As for His saying ﴿إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةٌ لاَّ ذَلُولٌ تُثِيرُ ٱلأَرْضَ وَلاَ تَسْقِي ٱلْحَرْثَ﴾ ﴿مُسَلَّمَةٌ﴾: "مسلمة" is on [the basis of] "إنَّها بَقَرَةٌ مُسَلَّمةٌ" ("it is a cow, sound").

akhfash:71-71.t:
﴿لاَّ شِيَةَ فِيهَا﴾: He is saying "there is no marking in it", from "وَشَيْتُ شِيَةً" ("I marked a marking"), just as you say "وَدَيْتُه دِيَةً" ("I paid him blood-money") and "وَعَدْتُهُ عِدَةً" ("I made him a promise").
And when you begin with (ألآن) [i.e. start reading from it], you pronounce both alifs with hamza, because the first alif is like the alif of "الرَّجل", and that one is pronounced when one begins with it, and the other is a fixed hamza; you say "ألآن", pronouncing the connecting alif. Some of them drop it and keep the wāw that is in (قَالُوا), because he used to drop it only because of the sukūn of the lām, and the lām has received a vowel, because the vowel of the hamza has been transferred to it.

akhfash:72-72.t: As for His saying ﴿وَإِذْ قَتَلْتُمْ نَفْساً فَٱدَّارَأْتُمْ فِيهَا﴾: it is only "فَتَدارَأْتُم", but the tāʾ is sometimes assimilated, as here, into the dāl, because its point of articulation is [close to] the point of articulation of the other. When it was assimilated into it, it was converted and made a dāl like it, and it was given sukūn, so they put an alif before it so as to be able to begin speaking with it, just as they said "اضرْب": they added the alif when the ḍād was quiescent. Do you not see that when you begin [with it] you say "ادّارأتم"? Similar to it are ﴿يَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾, ﴿تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ [and] ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَدَّبَّرُواْ ٱلْقَوْلَ﴾, and there is much like it in the Quran. It is only "يَتدَبَّرون", and the tāʾ was assimilated into the dāl because the tāʾ is close in point of articulation to the dāl: the point of articulation of the dāl is the tip of the tongue and the edges of the two front teeth, and the point of articulation of the tāʾ is the tip of the tongue and the roots of the two front teeth. So with everything whose point of articulation is close, do this; but do not say "يَنّزَّلون" for "يَتَنَزَّلون", because the nūn is not one of the letters of the front teeth like the tāʾ.

akhfash:208-208.t:
He said: ﴿ٱدْخُلُواْ فِي ٱلسِّلْمِ كَآفَّةً﴾, and "السِّلْمُ" is Islam. His saying ﴿وَتَدْعُوۤاْ إِلَى ٱلسَّلْمِ وَأَنتُمُ ٱلأَعْلَوْنَ﴾ — that is peace-making. Some have said "السِّلم" for peace-making. And He said ﴿وَيُلْقُوۤاْ إِلَيْكُمُ ٱلسَّلَمَ﴾, which is surrender. And He said ﴿وَإِذَا خَاطَبَهُمُ الجَاهِلُونَ قَالُواْ سَلاَماً﴾, that is: they said "[we declare our] freedom from you", because "السَّلام" in some speech is disassociation (barāʾa). You say "إنّما فلانٌ سَلامٌ بِسلام" ("So-and-so is only peace for peace"), that is: he mixes with no one. The poet said [in the wāfir metre; it is the one hundred and forty-first shāhid (attested verse)]:
سَلامَكَ رَبَّنا في كلِّ فَجْرٍ * بَريئا ما تَغَنَّثُكَ* الذُّمومُ
(We declare Your freedom [from all fault], our Lord, at every dawn — free, blame does not attach to You.)
He means "تَأَوَّبكَ" (comes back to You); he is saying "[we declare] Your freedom". And He said ﴿إِذْ دَخَلُواْ عَلَيْهِ فَقَالُواْ سَلاَماً قَالَ سَلاَمٌ﴾; this, according to what the exegetes claim, [means]: they said something good. It is as though — and Allah knows best — he heard affirmation of the Divine Oneness from them, so they had said something good; and when he knew that they were monotheists he said "Peace be upon you" and greeted them. In this sense it is nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject). Some said: "Whatever is from the speech of the angels is accusative, and whatever is from a human is nominative, in the [word] salām." This is weak and is no proof. And He said ﴿فَٱصْفَحْ عَنْهُمْ وَقُلْ سَلاَمٌ﴾; this is permissible in the meaning "peace be upon you" as a greeting, or it may be in the sense of disassociation, except that He made it the khabar (predicate) of a mubtadaʾ, as though He had said "My stance is salām", that is: my stance is disassociation from you; and He left the noun implied just as the khabar is left implied. The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the fourteenth shāhid]:
فَيا ظَبْيَةَ الوَعْساءِ بَيْنَ جَلاجِلٍ * وَبَينَ النَّقا آأَنْتِ أَمْ أُمُ سالِمِ
(O gazelle of the soft sands between Jalājil and al-Naqā — is it you, or Umm Sālim?)
On [the meaning]: "Is it you who are she, or Umm Sālim?", that is: you have confused me by Umm Sālim's resemblance to you. In all of this the khabar has been left implied. Like that is ﴿لاَ يَسْتَوِي مِنكُم مَّنْ أَنفَقَ مِن قَبْلِ ٱلْفَتْحِ وَقَاتَلَ أُوْلَـٰئِكَ أَعْظَمُ دَرَجَةً مِّنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَنفَقُواْ مِن بَعْدُ وَقَاتَلُواْ﴾: when He said ﴿أُوْلَـٰئِكَ أَعْظَمُ دَرَجَةً مِّنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَنفَقُواْ مِن بَعْدُ وَقَاتَلُواْ﴾, there was in it an indication of the meaning ﴿لاَ يَسْتَوِي مِنكُم مَّنْ أَنفَقَ مِن قَبْلِ ٱلْفَتْحِ﴾ "and whoever spent after the victory", that is: these and those are not equal.
And He said: ﴿وَلاَ تَتَّبِعُواْ خُطُوَاتِ ٱلشَّيْطَانِ﴾, because every light noun on the pattern "فُعْلَة", when it is pluralised, has its second letter vowelled with ḍamma, such as "ظُلُمات" and "غُرُفات", since when the two letters are articulated with one sound, one being close to its companion, [it is] easier for them. Some have given it fatḥa, saying "الرُكَبات", "الغُرفاَت" and "الظُلُمات" [Translator's note: so in the text; with fatḥa on the second letter these would be al-rukabāt, al-ghurafāt, al-ẓulamāt]. Some made quiescent what has wāw, just as what has yāʾ is made quiescent, such as "كُلْيات": he made the lām quiescent so that the yāʾ would not turn into a wāw, and so he made it quiescent in "خُطْوات", since the wāw is the sister of the yāʾ. Whatever is on the pattern "فَعْلة", such as "سَلْوَة" and "شَهْوَة", has its second letter vowelled with fatḥa in the plural, such as "سَلَوات" and "شَهَوات". When its first letter has kasra, its second letter takes kasra, such as "كِسْره" – "كِسِرات" and "سِدْرة" – "سِدِرات". Some gave the second letter of this fatḥa, just as they gave fatḥa to the second letter of the ḍamma-type, finding the two ḍammas and the two kasras heavy. Whatever of this kind has a wāw or yāʾ as its second letter, or in which two letters of the same kind meet, is not vowelled, such as "دُوْمَة" – "دُومات", "عُوذَة" – "عوذات" (that is, an amulet), "بَيْضَة" – "بَيْضات" and "مَيْتةَ" – "مَيْتات"; because if this were vowelled it would change and become alif, which would alter the structure of the noun, and they found that heavy. And they said "عِضَةٌ" – "عِضات" and did not vowel [the second letter], because this is a place where the lām of the root is vowelled, so it is not doubled; and were it not vowelled it would be doubled. Most [of what occurs] in "الظُلُمات", "الكِسِرات" and the like is that the second letter is vowelled according to the first. That led them to say "أذْكُر" [i.e. Udhkur], giving the alif ḍamma because of the ḍamma of the kāf, with a letter between them, and so that is more fitting. Some have said "أَنَا أُنْبُوك" ("I inform you") and "أَنا أُجُوك" ("I come to you"), giving the bāʾ and the jīm ḍamma because of the ḍamma of the hamza, to put them on one sound; this is more extreme than that. And [one] said "هذا هُو مُنْحَدُرٌ من الجَبَل" ("this is a descent from the mountain"), meaning "مُنْحَدَرٌ", giving the dāl ḍamma because of the ḍamma of the rāʾ, just as he gave ḍamma to the bāʾ and the jīm in "أُنْبُوكَ" and "أُجُوكَ".

akhfash:210-210.t: He said: ﴿هَلْ يَنظُرُونَ إِلاَّ أَن يَأْتِيَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ فِي ظُلَلٍ مِّنَ ٱلْغَمَامِ وَٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةُ﴾, on [the meaning] "and in the angels". [Translator's note: the explanations appear reversed in the text: "and in the angels" fits the genitive reading ﴿وَٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةِ﴾, while "and the angels come to them" fits the nominative.] Some read ﴿وَٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةِ﴾, that is: and the angels come to them. The nominative is the [correct] way and it is how we read, because He has said that in more than one place: He said ﴿وَجَآءَ رَبُّكَ وَٱلْمَلَكُ﴾ and He said ﴿إِلاَّ أَن تَأْتِيهُمُ ٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةُ أَوْ يَأْتِيَ رَبُّكَ﴾. "المَلَكُ" in this place is a collective, as you say "أَهْلَكَ الناسَ الدينارُ والدرهَمُ" ("the dinar and the dirham have destroyed people") and "هَلَكَ البَعِيرُ والشَّاءُ" ("the camel and the sheep perished"), meaning the whole body of camels and sheep. His saying ﴿إِلاَّ أَن يَأْتِيَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ﴾ means His command, because Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, does not move from place to place; just as you say "قَدْ خَشِينا أنْ تَأْتِينَا بنُو أُمَيَّة" ("we feared that the Banū Umayya would come to us"), and you mean only their rule.

akhfash:213-213.t: He said: ﴿وَمَا ٱخْتَلَفَ فِيهِ إِلاَّ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوهُ مِن بَعْدِ مَا جَآءَتْهُمُ ٱلْبَيِّنَاتُ بَغْياً بَيْنَهُمْ﴾. He is saying: "And none differed over it except those who were given it, out of envy among themselves, after the clear proofs had come to them."

akhfash:216-216.t: He said: ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْقِتَالُ وَهُوَ كُرْهٌ لَّكُمْ﴾. Some read ﴿حَمَلَتْهُ أُمه كَرْها﴾ and some read ﴿كُرْها﴾; they are two dialect forms, like "الغُسْل" and "الغَسْل", and "الضُعْف" and "الضَّعْف"; except that some have said that when it is in the position of the maṣdar (verbal noun) it is "كُرْهاً" [Translator's note: so in the text; the example that follows uses كَرْهاً with fatḥa], as you say "لا تقوم الا كَرْهاً" ("you do not stand up except unwillingly") and you say "لا تقوم الا على كُرْهٍ" ("you do not stand up except with reluctance"); and they are the same, like "الرُّهْبِ" and "الرَّهْبِ"; some said "الرَّهَب", just as they said "البُخْل", "البَخْل" and "البَخَل". He said ﴿كُرْهٌ لَكُم﴾ only [in the sense]: something of aversion; He omitted "ذو", as He said ﴿وَسْئَلِ ٱلْقَرْيَةَ﴾.

akhfash:217-217.t:
He said: ﴿وَصَدٌّ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ﴾.
And He said: ﴿وَكُفْرٌ بِهِ وَٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ﴾, on [the meaning] "and turning away from the Sacred Mosque".
Then He said: ﴿وَإِخْرَاجُ أَهْلِهِ مِنْهُ أَكْبَرُ﴾, as a mubtadaʾ (subject).
And He said: ﴿وَمَن يَرْتَدِدْ مِنكُمْ عَن دِينِهِ فَيَمُتْ وَهْوَ كَافِرٌ فَأُوْلۤـٰئِكَ حَبِطَتْ أَعْمَالُهُمْ﴾, separating the doubled letters, because the people of the Ḥijāz, when the lām of the root is quiescent, separate them; and here it is quiescent, made so by the conditional (jazāʾ). And He said ﴿وَمَنْ يَرْتَدَّ مِنْكُمْ عَنْ دِينِهِ فَسَوْفَ﴾, without separating, in the dialect of those who do not separate, because those who do not separate are many.

akhfash:219-219.t:
He said: ﴿وَيَسْأَلُونَكَ مَاذَا يُنفِقُونَ قُلِ ٱلْعَفْوَ﴾, if you make ﴿ماذا﴾ equivalent to (ما). If you make ﴿ماذا﴾ equivalent to "الذي" (that which), you say ﴿قُلْ ٱلْعَفْوُ﴾. The first is accusative and this one nominative, as though he had said ﴿ما الذي يُنْفِقُون﴾ ("what is it that they spend?") and He said: "What they spend is the surplus". When you put it in the accusative, it is as though he had said "What do they spend?" and He said: "They spend the surplus", because when ﴿ما﴾ is not made equivalent to "الذي", "العَفْو" is accusative by "يُنْفِقُون"; and if it is made equivalent to "الذي", it is nominative as the khabar (predicate) of the mubtadaʾ. Just as He said ﴿مَّاذَآ أَنْزَلَ رَبُّكُمْ قَالُواْ أَسَاطِيرُ ٱلأَوَّلِينَ﴾, making ﴿مَّاذَآ﴾ equivalent to "الذي", and said ﴿مَاذَا أَنْزَلَ رَبُّكُمْ قَالُواْ خَيْراً﴾, making ﴿ماذا﴾ equivalent to "ما". When one makes it equivalent to "ما" alone, the nominative may also occur according to the meaning; for if someone were asked "What did you do?" and he said "Good" (nominative), that is: what I did is good, there would be nothing wrong with it. And if you used the accusative when making "ذا" equivalent to "الذي", it would also be good; for if you were asked "What is it that you did?" and you said "Good" (accusative), that is: I did good, it would be correct. The poet said [in the wāfir metre; it is the thirtieth shāhid]:
دَعِي ماذا عَلِمْتُ سَأَتَّقِيهِ * ولكِنْ بِالمُغَيَّبِ نَبئِّيني
(Leave what I already know — I shall guard against it — but tell me of what is hidden.)
He made "ما" and "ذا" equivalent to "ما" alone; "ذا" cannot be equivalent to "الذي" in this verse, because if you said "دعي ما الذي علمت" it would not be [proper] speech. The exegetes said concerning His saying ﴿مَاذَا أَنْزَلَ رَبُّكُمْ قَالُوا أَسَاطِيرُ ٱلأَوَّلِينَ ﴾: [it is so] because the disbelievers denied that their Lord had sent down anything, so they said to them: "What you say is the legends of the ancients", that is: "that which you say is the legends of the ancients" — not on [the meaning] "our Lord sent down the legends of the ancients". This meaning, as we see it — and Allah knows best — is like His saying ﴿وَإِنْ تُخَالِطُوهُمْ فَإِخْوَانُكُمْ﴾, that is: then they are your brothers.

akhfash:222-222.t:
He said: ﴿ وَيَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلْمَحِيضِ﴾, which is menstruation. Most usage in the maṣdar (verbal noun), when it is formed like this, is that "مَفْعَل" is intended, such as your saying "ما في بُرِّكَ مَكَالٌ" ("there is no measuring in your wheat"), that is: measuring. The other form has also been said, that is, "مَكِيلٌ" was said; it is like "مَحِيضٍ" from the verb when it is a maṣdar, as in the one in the Qur'an, and it is less frequent. The poet said [in the kāmil metre; it is the one hundred and forty-second shāhid]:
بُنِيَتْ مَرافِقُهُنَّ فَوْقَ مَزِلَّةٍ * لا يَسْتَطِيعُ بِها القُرادُ مقيلا
(Their elbows are built above a slippery place on which a tick cannot manage a midday rest.)
He means "قَيْلُولَةً" (a midday rest). And you say "جِئْتُ مَجيئاً حَسَناً" ("I came a fine coming"); they formed it on "مَفْعِل", and it is its maṣdar.
And He said: ﴿وَلاَ تَقْرَبُوهُنَّ حَتَّىٰ يَطْهُرْنَ﴾, because you say "طَهَرَتْ المرأةُ" ("the woman became pure"), so "هِيَ تَطْهُرُ"; some said "طَهُرَت". They said "طَلَقَتْ", "تَطْلُق" and also "طَلُقَت", "تَطْلُقُ". It is said of a woman in childbirth when the bleeding of childbirth comes upon her: "نُفِسَت"; and when labour pains come upon her, [it is said]:
"طُلِقَتْ".

akhfash:225-225.t: He said: ﴿لاَّ يُؤَاخِذُكُمُ ٱللَّهُ بِٱلَّلغْوِ فِيۤ أَيْمَانِكُمْ﴾. We say "لَغَوْتُ في اليمين" ("I spoke idly in the oath"), so "أَنا أَلغْو" "لَغْواً"; and whoever says "هو يَمْحا" ("he erases") says "هَو يَلْغا", "لَغْواً" and "مَحْواً". We have heard that from the Arabs. And you say "لَغِيتُ باسمِ فلانٍ", so "أَنَا ألْغى به" "لَغَى", that is: I mention him [constantly].

akhfash:226-226.t: He said: ﴿لِّلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِن نِّسَآئِهِمْ﴾. You say "آلى مِن امرأَتِهِ" ("he swore off his wife"), "يُؤْلي", "إيْلاءً", and "ظاهَرَ مِنْها", "ظِهاراً", just as you say "قاتَلَ", "قِتالاً". ﴿تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ أَشْهُرٍ﴾ ﴿لِّلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ﴾: He made that a term for them. ﴿فَإِنْ فَآءُوا﴾ means: "then if they return", because you say "فِئْتُ إلى الحَقِّ" ("I returned to the truth").

akhfash:228-228.t:
He said: ﴿ثَلاَثَةَ قُرُوۤءٍ﴾, lengthened and with hamza. Its singular is "القَرْءُ", light and with hamza, like "القَرْع". You say "قَدْ أَقْرَأَتِ المَرأَةُ", "إِقْراءً", with hamza, when she has come to menstruate. You say "ما قَرَأَتْ حَيْضَةً قَطْ" ("she has never had a menstruation") like "ما قَرَأَتْ قُرآناً" ("she has never recited a Qur'an"), and "قَدْ قَرَأَتْ حَيْضَةً أَوْ حَيْضتَيْنِ" ("she has had one or two menstruations"), with hamza; and "ما قَرَأَتْ جَنِينا قطُّ" is like it, that is: she has never been pregnant. And "القَرْءُ" is the cessation of menstruation. Some said: what is between the two menstruations. The poet said [in the wāfir metre; it is the one hundred and forty-third shāhid]:
ذِراعَيْ بَكْرَةٍ أَدْماء بَكْرٍ * هِجانِ اللَّوْنِ لَمْ تَقْرأ جَنينا
(The two forelegs of a young, light-tawny she-camel, a first-born, of pure white colour, who has never carried a foetus.)
As for the poet's saying [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the one hundred and forty-fourth shāhid]:
فَتُوضِحَ فالمِقراةَ لَمْ يَعْفُ رَسْمُها * لِما نَسَجَتْها مِنْ جَنُوبٍ وَشَمْأَلِ
(Then Tūḍiḥ and al-Miqrāt, whose traces have not been effaced by what the south and north winds have woven over them.)
"المِقرْاة" is a watercourse, and it does not have hamza.

akhfash:232-232.t:
He said: ﴿فَلاَ تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ﴾: He forbids their [former] husbands from preventing them from [marrying] husbands.
And He said ﴿ذٰلِكَ يُوعَظُ بِهِ﴾ and ﴿ذٰلِكُمْ أَزْكَىٰ لَكُمْ وَأَطْهَرُ﴾, because He addressed men; and He said in another place "ذلِكُنَّ الذي لُمْتُنَّني فيه" because He addressed women. Had He left "ذلك" without attaching to it [the pronouns of] those He addressed, it would have been permissible. He said ﴿مَن يَأْتِ مِنكُنَّ بِفَاحِشَةٍ مُّبَيِّنَةٍ يُضَاعَفْ لَهَا ٱلْعَذَابُ ضِعْفَيْنِ وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ يَسِيراً﴾ and did not say ﴿ذَلِكُنَّ﴾; and He said ﴿فَٱسْتَبْشِرُواْ بِبَيْعِكُمُ ٱلَّذِي بَايَعْتُمْ بِهِ وَذَلِكَ هُوَ ٱلْفَوْزُ ٱلْعَظِيمُ﴾. And He said in al-Mujādila ﴿ذَلِكَ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ وَأَطْهَرُ﴾. This is no more far-fetched than His saying ﴿حَتَّىٰ إِذَا كُنتُمْ فِي ٱلْفُلْكِ وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِم﴾, where He addressed [them] and then spoke of the absent, because the absent is the present one in this place. And He said ﴿هَلْ أُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِشَرٍّ مِّن ذٰلِكَ مَثُوبَةً﴾.

akhfash:233-233.t:
He said: ﴿حَوْلَيْنِ كَامِلَيْنِ لِمَنْ أَرَادَ أَن يُتِمَّ ٱلرَّضَاعَةَ﴾, because one says "بيني وَبَيْنَكَ رَضاعَةٌ" ("there is a suckling relationship between me and you") and "رَضاعٌ"; and you say "اللُّؤمُ والرَّضاعَةُ" (meanness and [its kind of] suckling); it has fatḥa in every case. Some of Banū Tamīm give it kasra when it refers to suckling, saying "الرِّضاعة".
And He said: ﴿لاَ تُكَلَّفُ نَفْسٌ إِلاَّ وُسْعَهَا لاَ تُضَآرَّ وَالِدَةٌ﴾: nominative as a statement. He is saying: "Thus it is in the ruling that a mother is not to be harmed on account of her child"; he is saying "it is proper (يَنْبَغي)", and when "يَنْبَغي" was omitted and "تُضارُّ" came in its place, it took its form. Like it is ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنكُمْ وَيَذَرُونَ أَزْوَاجاً﴾: the khabar of ﴿وَٱلَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ﴾ is ﴿يَتَرَبَّصْنَ﴾ "after their death", and He did not mention "after their death", just as part of speech is omitted. He is saying: "It is proper for them to wait"; and when "يَنْبغي" was omitted, "يَتَرَبَّصْنَ" fell into its place. The poet said [in the ṭawīl metre; it is the one hundred and forty-fifth shāhid]:
على الحَكَمِ المَأْتِيِّ يَوْماً إذا قضى * قَضِيَّتَهُ أنْ لا يَجُورَ وَيَقْصِدُ
(It is incumbent on the arbiter who is approached one day, when he gives his judgement, not to be unjust, and he should be moderate.)
He put "وَيَقْصِدُ" in the nominative on [the meaning of] his saying "and it is proper". Whoever takes ﴿لاَ تُضَآرّ﴾ as a prohibition reads ﴿لاَ تُضَآرَّ﴾ with fatḥa; this is in the dialect of those who do not separate the doubled letters. As for those who separate, they say ﴿لا تضارَرْ﴾ when they mean the prohibition, because the lām of the root is quiescent when you say "لا تُفاعَلْ" while forbidding. However, "تضارَ" here is not separated, because there is only one rāʾ in the written text.

akhfash:22-22.t: His words ﴿فَلاَ تَجْعَلُواْ للَّهِ أَندَاداً﴾: He made the alif disjunctive (alif qaṭʿ) because it is a noun in which the alif remains in the diminutive: [so] when you make it diminutive you say "أُنَيْداداً"*. [Translator's note: the asterisk appears thus in the source.] The singular of "الأنْداد" is "نِدٌّ", and "النِدُّ" means a likeness (equal).

akhfash:24-24.t: His words ﴿ٱلَّتِي وَقُودُهَا ٱلنَّاسُ وَٱلْحِجَارَةُ﴾: "الوَقُودُ"** is firewood, and "الوُقودُ" is the burning, which is the act (maṣdar). [Translator's note: the asterisks appear thus in the source.] It is read ﴿الوَقود﴾ and ﴿الوُقود﴾, and it may mean firewood, and it may mean the act. Similar to that is "الوَضُوءُ", which is the water [for ablution], and "الوُضُوءُ", which is the act; and they claimed that they are two dialect forms with one meaning.

akhfash:25-25.t:
His words ﴿أَنَّ لَهُمْ جَنَّاتٍ تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِهَا ٱلأَنْهَارُ﴾: He gave "جناتٍ" the genitive ending (kasra) although "أَنَّ" governs it [in the accusative], because every plural that has at its end an added tāʾ, which goes in the singular and in its diminutive, has its accusative [marked] as the genitive. Do you not see that you say "جَنّه" (a garden) and the tāʾ goes? And He said ﴿خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَاوَاتِ وَٱلأَرْضَ﴾: "السماوات" has the genitive ending and "الأرضَ" is accusative, because the tāʾ is added; do you not see that you say "سماء"? [Translator's note: the verse is quoted with "الأرضَ" in the accusative to illustrate that "السماوات" is accusative by position.] And ﴿قَالُواْ رَبَّنَآ إِنَّآ أَطَعْنَا سَادَتَنَا وَكُبَرَآءَنَا﴾ [has fatḥa], because this is not a tāʾ; it is a hāʾ that became a tāʾ in connected speech, and it is that [hāʾ] in the pause. Do you not see that you say "رأيتُ سادَه" (I saw the chiefs), with no tāʾ in it? Whoever read ﴿أَطَعْنا سَادَاتِنا﴾ gave it the genitive ending, because when you say "ساده" the tāʾ goes; and in the pause it has a tāʾ: you say "رأيت ساداتٍ". [Translator's note: so in the source.] They gave this the genitive ending in the accusative only to make its genitive and accusative one, just as its masculine [plural] was made one in the genitive and accusative: you say "مسلمين" and "صالحين", its accusative and genitive with yāʾ. As for His words ﴿بُيُوتاً غَيْرَ بُيُوتِكُمْ﴾ and ﴿لاَ تَرْفَعُوۤاْ أَصْوَاتَكُمْ﴾, the tāʾ belongs to the root of the word: you say "صوت" and "صويت" and the tāʾ does not go, and "بيت" [and "بُوَيْت"]* and the tāʾ does not go.
